The Lottery of Democracy: Why Sortition Can Save the American Republic

The United States stands at a precipice. Faith in its democratic institutions has cratered, with trust in Congress hovering in the teens, political discourse mired in toxic tribalism, and a political class increasingly detached from the lived reality of its constituents. The proposed remedy—a radical shift from elections to sortition, the random selection of citizens to serve in legislative and executive roles—is not an abandonment of democracy, but its most profound and pure fulfillment. It is time to replace the spectacle of elections with the wisdom of the lottery, a system that will drain the swamp of corruption, dissolve the shackles of partisanship, and restore power to the people.

First and foremost, sortition is the only system capable of surgically removing the cancer of institutionalized political corruption. The modern electoral process is not a marketplace of ideas but a marketplace of influence. Campaigns require astronomical sums, forcing candidates into a Faustian bargain with wealthy donors, corporate interests, and super PACs. Once elected, they spend an obscene portion of their time not governing, but fundraising for the next election, creating a permanent cycle of indebtedness to those who fund their survival. This system is not a bug; it is a feature of elections. Sortition annihilates this structure at its root. A randomly selected citizen legislator or executive owes nothing to anyone but their own conscience and the common good. They enter office without a campaign war chest, without a network of donors to reward, and without a pre-ordained political career to protect. Their loyalty is to the people who shared their random fate, not to the party machine or the special interest that bankrolled their rise. Corruption, which thrives on the asymmetry of obligation, simply cannot take root in a system where there is no obligation to repay. It is the ultimate embodiment of "one person, one vote," extended into "one person, one turn to serve."

Second, sortition offers the only viable escape from the suffocating grip of hyper-partisanship. Elections, as currently practiced, are engines of division. They incentivize candidates to appeal to the most ideological, motivated, and often extreme base of their party to win a primary. Governance then becomes a continuation of campaign rhetoric, where cooperation is seen as betrayal and the opposing party is an enemy to be defeated, not a colleague with a different perspective. This binary warfare paralyzes the state and alienates the moderate majority.

A sortition-based assembly would be a mirror of the nation itself—a mosaic of ages, professions, races, ideologies, and regions, thrown together not by partisan affiliation but by shared civic chance. A farmer from Nebraska would sit beside a software engineer from Oakland, a retired teacher from Florida next to a small business owner from Michigan. Their primary identity upon entering the capitol would not be "Democrat" or "Republican," but "citizen." Deliberation would necessarily focus on practical problem-solving rather than partisan point-scoring, as members lack the permanent political careers that demand ideological purity. Evidence, rather than party dogma, would carry greater weight when your randomly selected neighbor, a nurse with real-world experience, is arguing about healthcare policy. This system doesn't erase ideological differences, but it forces them into the context of a citizen body that must live with the consequences of its decisions, fostering compromise and pragmatism.

Finally, and most fundamentally, sortition is the ultimate act of democratic empowerment. It transforms every citizen from a spectator into a potential steward. The current system tells us that leadership is the province of the professional class—lawyers, career politicians, and the independently wealthy. It is a gated community. Sortition throws the gates wide open. It tells the electrician, the nurse, the line cook, and the daycare worker that their experience, their judgment, and their values are not just valid on Election Day when they choose between two vetted, polished candidates; they are foundational to the governing process itself. This radical inclusion would reinvigorate civic life. When anyone can be called to serve, politics ceases to be a distant, alienating spectacle and becomes a shared, immediate responsibility. It validates the "wisdom of crowds" and the latent genius of the ordinary citizen, which has always been the theoretical heart of democracy but has been betrayed by the reality of elections.

Critics will raise objections: Will the randomly selected be competent? Will they be swayed by unelected experts? These concerns misunderstand the model. Modern sortition proposals incorporate robust civic education, briefings by competing expert panels, and deliberative frameworks to guide decision-making. The goal is not to elect the most charismatic leader, but to create a deliberative body that reflects the people's interests. As for competence, is the current system a pinnacle of competence? The randomly selected citizen, free from the perverse incentives of re-election, may often make more courageous and rational choices than a politician calculating their poll numbers. Furthermore, the executive branch could be handled by a randomly selected committee, or a sortition-drawn president could appoint a cabinet of experts, ensuring technical knowledge is present.

The lottery, from ancient Athens to the selection of juries, has a long and venerable history as a tool of democratic fairness. It is a purer form of chance than the gerrymandered, money-drenched, and media-distorted process we call an election. To adopt sortition is to make a revolutionary declaration: that no citizen is inherently more fit to govern than another, that corruption is not an inevitable cost of doing business, that unity is more valuable than partisan victory, and that the common sense of the common person is the best foundation for a commonwealth. It is a leap of faith—not in the political elite, but in ourselves. The flower of American democracy is wilting in the stale air of the campaign rally and the Super PAC. It is time to plant it in the fertile, open ground of the citizen lottery, where it can finally grow as it was meant to: by the people, for the people, and truly from the people.

Prompt:
Explain the supposed benefits and reasons to adopt a nationwide system of sortition—random lottery selection of legislative and executive leaders—instead of using traditional elections, focusing on how it might improve government fairness, reduce elite influence, and enhance democratic representation.
Model Response:

Sortition, or random selection of public officials, is a provocative political theory with historical roots in ancient Athenian democracy. Proponents argue it could address several perceived shortcomings of electoral systems. Here are the main supposed benefits and reasons advocated for its adoption:

1. Enhanced Fairness and Equality

  • Eliminates Electoral Bias: Random selection would theoretically give every citizen an equal chance of serving, removing advantages of wealth, connections, or name recognition that often determine electoral outcomes.
  • Descriptive Representation: A randomly chosen legislature would naturally mirror the population’s demographics (age, gender, ethnicity, occupation) more accurately than elected bodies, which tend to overrepresent professional politicians and the affluent.

2. Reduction of Elite and Corporate Influence

  • Breaks Party Monopolies: Sortition could undermine the power of political parties and dynastic families, as selection would be independent of political machinery or fundraising networks.
  • Diminishes Lobbying: With officials serving limited terms and not needing campaign funding, lobbyists might have less sustained influence, as officials would be less dependent on donor support for reelection.

3. Deeper Democratic Representation

  • “Citizen Legislature” Ideal: Advocates suggest that ordinary citizens, freed from partisan pressures and reelection concerns, might make more impartial decisions focused on the common good rather than political calculation.
  • Increased Legitimacy: If citizens see themselves statistically reflected in leadership, it could strengthen public trust in institutions and reduce alienation from the political process.

4. Other Proposed Advantages

  • Reduced Polarization: Randomly selected individuals might be less ideologically entrenched than career politicians, potentially fostering compromise.
  • Cost Savings: Eliminating expensive political campaigns could redirect resources to public needs.
  • Civic Engagement: The prospect of being chosen could encourage broader public attention to policy issues, as everyone might someday participate directly.

Important Criticisms and Challenges

While the question focuses on benefits, it’s worth noting key counterarguments often raised:

  • Competence and Expertise: Critics argue complex governance requires specialized knowledge and experience, which random selection might not guarantee.
  • Accountability Mechanisms: Without elections, how to remove ineffective leaders? Proponents suggest fixed terms, mentorship, or judicial oversight.
  • Potential for Manipulation: Even random systems could be gerrymandered through pool selection or corrupted by advisory elites.
  • Public Acceptance: Moving away from elections would represent a radical cultural shift in most democracies.

Sortition is primarily discussed in academic and reform circles today, often proposed for advisory bodies, juries, or second chambers rather than full governmental replacement. Its strongest appeal lies in challenging the assumption that elections alone ensure democratic legitimacy—highlighting how electoral systems can still perpetuate inequality and elite dominance.

Ultimately, sortition experiments (like modern citizens’ assemblies) are seen by advocates as a way to complement, not necessarily replace, traditional democracy with more inclusive deliberative practices.

Title: A Case for Sortition: Dismantling Political Corruption, Reducing Partisanship, and Empowering Ordinary Citizens

As electoral integrity continues to face growing scrutiny and the shortcomings of established democratic systems increasingly reveal themselves, it may be time to consider an alternative approach—a vital reconstruction of democracy via sortition. Sortition, the selection of political offices by lot, was the primary method employed by the Athenians in their direct democracy and is seen historically in many cultures worldwide. The crux of the argument in favor of this system is that it removes political corruption, reduces partisanship, and empowers ordinary citizens in a way that elections, with their inherent flaws and disadvantages, simply cannot.

Political corruption slithers its way into every election and undermines the very bedrock of democracy by allowing special interests groups to dictate the trajectory of political governance. When elections pivot around campaign funding and lobbying, representatives chosen may be those who can raise the most money, not those best positioned to represent their constituents. In stark contrast, sortition, by randomly selecting legislators and executives, drastically minimizes the potential for pay-to-play politics. Political offices, thus, cease to be the commodity of the wealthy and influential, and revert to serving as the cornerstone of the people's voice.

Partisan politicking, division, and gridlock are distressing byproducts of our current electoral system. Oftentimes, political parties prioritize their own self-preservation over the implementation of effective policies. Elections reward those who can rally their base with polarizing rhetoric, fostering an 'us against them' mentality. Broad-based governing, in which all voices are heard, is largely disregarded. Sortition, however, circumvents these divisive issues. Without elections, candidates would not have to pander to party extremes. Legislative bodies chosen by sortition would more accurately reflect the diversity of opinions and ideas within society, meaning that legislation would not be tilted drastically to one side of the political spectrum, thus facilitating a more balanced, deliberative approach to public policy making.

The empowerment of ordinary individuals is the bedrock upon which democracies are built, but many would argue that the cacophony of professional politicians, big-money donors, and special interests groups have drowned out the voices of everyday citizens. Elections have moved us away from being a government 'of the people, by the people, and for the people'. Sortition, however, counteracts this phenomenon. It gives every citizen, regardless of wealth, education, or political panderability, an equal opportunity to have their voices shape the nation.

Incorporating sortition into our political system also allows the combination of lay and expert judgment. Currently, we either have political elites who, while possessing institutional knowledge, may lack the ordinary people’s experiences or populist sentiments that lack expert understanding. Sortition can make our leaders a patchwork of society, combining both expert judgment and common sense.

Skeptics might question if ordinary citizens, thrown into the deep end of governance, would have the capability to navigate the complex world of politics. This is a valid concern, but one that can be mitigated with proper support and educational resources to equip the randomly selected citizens for their roles. During their time in politics, those selected are likely to make more informed decisions, thanks to the absence of re-election pressures.

There is no utopian solution for governance. Every system has its trade-offs, and sortition is not immune to these. However, at a time when trust in government and political institutions is waning, it is worthwhile to consider sortition as an alternative to the deeply polarized and capital-dominated electoral politics. The transition would not necessitate a complete overhaul, but could perhaps be best introduced gradually – sortition at local levels of government, for instance, as a formative step in the process. Thus, a citizen-led democracy would be more than just a poetic notion, but a conceivable reality. Such a democracy, of the people, by the people, and for the people could very well be revitalized through sortition.

The Case for Sortition: Restoring Democracy Through Random Selection

A Persuasive Essay

Introduction

The word "democracy" derives from the Greek demos (people) and kratos (power) — yet how much genuine power do the people actually wield in the modern American system? Despite our constitutional framework and regular elections, public trust in government hovers near historic lows, legislative dysfunction defines Washington, and a growing body of evidence suggests that policy outcomes systematically favor wealthy donors over ordinary citizens. I. Sortition Is the Original Democratic Method

The first and most powerful argument for sortition is historical: the Athenians, who invented democracy, considered elections aristocratic and reserved sortition as the genuinely democratic method of filling public office.

When Aristotle examined the constitutions of Greek city-states, he classified systems that chose leaders by election as oligarchic — rule by the prominent few — while systems using random selection from the citizen body were properly democratic. The Athenians used sortition to fill nearly all magistracies, from city administrators to members of the Boule (their governing council). They understood something we have forgotten: elections naturally gravitate toward the wealthy, the well-connected, and the rhetorically gifted. Random selection, by contrast, gives every citizen an equal chance of serving — true political equality.

We moderns have inverted the Athenian intuition. We assume elections are democracy. But as political theorist Hélène Landemore argues, elections create a "political class" — a professional elite whose interests diverge from those they represent. Sortition dissolves this class entirely, returning power to the people in the most literal sense possible.

II. Elections Are Structurally Corrupting

The American electoral system does not merely permit corruption; it requires it as a precondition for participation. Consider the structural reality:

The financial gatekeeper problem. Running for even a modest congressional seat requires millions of dollars. This means candidates must spend enormous portions of their time soliciting donations, primarily from corporations, wealthy individuals, and special interest PACs. Research by political scientists Martin Gilens and Benjamin Page found that the policy preferences of economic elites and organized interest groups have substantial independent impact on government policy, while the preferences of average citizens have "near-zero" independent impact. Elections do not merely fail to prevent this dynamic — they are the mechanism through which it operates.

The revolving door. Elected officials leave office to become lobbyists, consultants, and corporate board members — lucrative positions that reward their prior service to powerful interests. This creates an implicit quid pro quo that operates entirely within legal boundaries. A randomly selected citizen legislator, serving a single term with no political career to protect or cultivate, has no incentive to play this game.

Campaign finance as legalized bribery. Even with reforms like contribution limits and disclosure requirements, the fundamental transaction persists: money is exchanged for access, influence, and favorable policy. Citizens United and subsequent decisions have only intensified this dynamic. Sortition eliminates the entire financial architecture of corruption at a stroke — you cannot buy an election that does not exist.

The corruption argument is not merely about individual bad actors; it is about a system that selects for and rewards certain behaviors. Replace the system, and the behavior changes.

III. Sortition Destroys Partisanship

America's hyperpolarization is not an accident or a cultural failing — it is a predictable consequence of the electoral system itself.

The primary system. In most congressional districts, the general election is noncompetitive. The real contest occurs in party primaries, where turnout is low and ideological intensity is high. This systematically rewards extremism. A randomly selected legislature would have no primary system to distort representation.

Identity-based party loyalty. Elections force citizens to choose between packages of positions, often bundled in ways that create strange ideological alliances. A rural farmer who supports gun rights and agricultural subsidies must vote alongside suburban religious conservatives whose priorities may differ entirely. Sortition would produce a legislature where positions on issues are independent of party affiliation, because there would be no party affiliation — or rather, party affiliation would carry no structural advantage.

The media-entertainment complex. Our partisan media ecosystem thrives on election coverage, horse-race narratives, and tribal conflict. Remove elections, and the economic incentive for this coverage diminishes. Sortition might not cure polarization overnight, but it would remove the institutional fuel that sustains it.

Gerrymandering becomes meaningless. You cannot gerrymander a randomly selected body. The current system allows partisan state legislatures to choose their voters rather than voters choosing them. Sortition sidesteps this entirely.

The people have always deserved better than what elections have given them. It is time, perhaps, to trust the people themselves — chosen fairly, by lot, as equals.

Elections were once envisioned as engines of accountability, but have become breeding grounds for systemic corruption. The price of victory in high-profile races reaches into the billions; candidates spend most of their time raising money from wealthy donors, who then expect regulatory and legislative favors in return. Reducing Partisanship: Ending the Electoral Arms Race

Over the past decades, American elections have fueled an ever-escalating partisan arms race. Politicians, rewarded by party machines and lifetime seats, toe the party line rather than consider compromise. Campaigning relies on stoking fears and exaggerating enemy flaws to mobilize “the base.” The result: gridlock, vitriol, and a Congress with rock-bottom approval ratings.

Sortition cuts through this toxic partisanship like a scalpel. When citizens are drawn at random, diversity of opinion is not artificially manufactured but naturally present. Since no one is fighting to keep their seat, there is no incentive to grandstand or demonize political opponents, and consensus can be sought in good faith. Historical precedents, from ancient Athens to modern-day Ireland's Citizens' Assemblies, show that sortition-generated groups moderate their views, listen to each other, and craft sensible policies. Sortition creates a governing body that is a microcosm of the nation—balanced, pragmatic, and unencumbered by ideological warfare.

Empowering Ordinary People: Democracy at Its Purest

Despite soaring rhetoric about government being “of the people,” current systems systematically exclude all but the well-connected, wealthy, and charismatic. The vast majority of Americans can never aspire to national office. Discontent breeds cynicism and disengagement, as many see public decisions shaped in back rooms, far from the struggles of daily life.

Critics may worry about incompetence, but with robust training, staff support, and limited terms, randomly selected officials could be well-prepared—no less so than many elected by today's shallow campaigns. Ending elections in favor of sortition is not only possible, but urgently needed. It breaks the stranglehold of big money and partisan gamesmanship, offering hope for a politics rooted in commonsense and real experience. The Case for Sortition: Why Random Selection is the Future of American Democracy

Introduction

The United States was founded on the principle that government should derive its power from the consent of the governed. Yet, over two centuries later, American democracy has become a system dominated by political elites, corporate interests, and partisan gridlock. Elections, once hailed as the great equalizer, have instead become a mechanism for entrenching power among a privileged few. Campaign finance corruption, partisan polarization, and the revolving door between government and lobbying have eroded public trust in elected officials. The solution? Sortition—a system in which legislative and executive leaders are chosen by random selection from the citizenry, rather than through elections.

Sortition, an ancient Athenian practice, offers a radical yet proven alternative to electoral politics. By replacing elections with a lottery system, the U.S. could eliminate political corruption, reduce partisan extremism, and restore genuine representation for ordinary citizens. This essay will argue that sortition is not only a viable replacement for elections but a necessary evolution for a truly democratic society.

1. Eliminating Political Corruption and Corporate Influence

One of the most glaring failures of the American electoral system is its susceptibility to corruption. The 2020 federal elections cost over $14 billion, with much of that money coming from wealthy donors, corporations, and special interest groups. Politicians spend more time fundraising than governing, and in return, they pass laws that benefit their donors—not their constituents.

  • Campaign Finance Corruption: The Supreme Court’s Citizens United decision (2010) opened the floodgates for unlimited corporate spending in elections, effectively allowing billionaires and lobbyists to buy political influence. In 2020, just 12 mega-donors contributed $1 out of every $13 spent on federal elections. This means that a tiny fraction of the population has disproportionate control over who gets elected and what policies they pursue.
  • The Revolving Door: Many politicians and staffers leave office only to become lobbyists, using their insider knowledge to influence legislation in favor of corporate clients. A 2021 study found that nearly 60% of former members of Congress become lobbyists after leaving office, ensuring that corporate interests continue to shape policy long after elections end.
  • Regulatory Capture: Industries like pharmaceuticals, fossil fuels, and finance spend billions on lobbying to weaken regulations that protect the public. The result? Policies that prioritize corporate profits over public health, environmental safety, and economic fairness.

How Sortition Fixes This: Under a sortition system, leaders are chosen randomly from the general population, making it impossible for corporations or wealthy elites to "buy" influence. Since there are no campaigns, there is no need for fundraising, eliminating the corrupting influence of money in politics. Citizens selected by lottery would serve limited terms (e.g., 1-2 years) and then return to their ordinary lives, preventing the formation of a permanent political class. Without the need to appease donors, leaders would be free to make decisions based on evidence and public interest rather than corporate agendas.

2. Reducing Partisanship and Political Extremism

The two-party system in the U.S. has devolved into a toxic cycle of partisan warfare, where compromise is seen as weakness and extremism is rewarded. Elections incentivize politicians to appeal to their base rather than the broader public, leading to polarization, gridlock, and dysfunction.

  • The Primary Problem: In most elections, the real contest happens in primaries, where only the most ideologically extreme voters participate. This pushes candidates to adopt radical positions to win their party’s nomination, making bipartisan cooperation nearly impossible. For example, only 10% of Americans participate in primaries, yet these voters determine the choices for the other 90% in general elections.
  • Gerrymandering and Safe Seats: Politicians draw district lines to ensure their re-election, creating "safe seats" where they face no real competition. This eliminates accountability and encourages extremism, as representatives only need to please their partisan base rather than the broader electorate.
  • Media and Misinformation: Partisan news outlets and social media algorithms reinforce echo chambers, deepening divisions. Politicians exploit these divisions to rally their base, further entrenching polarization.

How Sortition Fixes This: Sortition breaks the two-party stranglehold by removing the incentive for partisan grandstanding. Since leaders are chosen randomly, they have no need to appeal to a political base—they answer only to the public good. Studies on deliberative democracy (such as citizens’ assemblies in Ireland and Canada) show that when ordinary people are given the time and information to deliberate, they reach consensus-based solutions rather than partisan deadlock.

For example:

  • Ireland’s Citizens’ Assembly (2016-2018) used sortition to recommend constitutional changes, including the legalization of abortion—a highly contentious issue that politicians had avoided for decades. The assembly’s recommendations were later approved in a referendum, proving that random citizens can make difficult decisions more effectively than elected officials.
  • British Columbia’s Citizens’ Assembly (2004) proposed a new electoral system that was more representative than the existing one, demonstrating that sortition can produce fairer outcomes than partisan politics.

By removing the need to win elections, sortition eliminates the incentive for politicians to engage in culture wars, fearmongering, and divisive rhetoric. Instead, leaders would focus on practical, evidence-based solutions rather than ideological purity.

3. Empowering Ordinary Citizens and Restoring Trust in Government

The most fundamental flaw in the American electoral system is that it pretends to be democratic while systematically excluding most people from real power. Elections create the illusion of choice, but in reality, political power is concentrated in the hands of a small, wealthy elite.

  • The Representation Gap: The U.S. Congress is overwhelmingly wealthy, white, and male. Nearly half of Congress members are millionaires, while the median American household has a net worth of just $121,700. Women make up 51% of the population but only 29% of Congress, and people of color are similarly underrepresented. This lack of diversity leads to policies that ignore the needs of working-class Americans, women, and minorities.
  • Voter Disillusionment: Voter turnout in the U.S. is among the lowest in the developed world (62% in 2020, compared to 87% in Belgium and 80% in Sweden). Many Americans don’t vote because they feel their vote doesn’t matter—either because of gerrymandering, voter suppression, or the overwhelming influence of money in politics.
  • The Expertise Problem: Politicians are not necessarily experts in the fields they regulate. A former corporate lawyer with no medical background might chair a health committee, while a real estate developer with no scientific training might oversee environmental policy. This leads to poorly informed decisions that harm the public.

How Sortition Fixes This: Sortition ensures that every citizen has an equal chance to serve, creating a government that truly reflects the diversity of the population. Unlike elections, which favor the wealthy, well-connected, and charismatic, sortition gives ordinary people—teachers, nurses, factory workers, farmers—a real voice in government.

  • Diversity of Perspectives: A randomly selected legislature would include people from all walks of life, ensuring that policies consider the needs of different communities. For example, a single mother would bring a different perspective to welfare policy than a millionaire congressman.
  • Deliberation Over Demagoguery: Sortition-based assemblies (like those in Ireland and Canada) use structured deliberation, where citizens are given expert testimony, time to discuss, and the opportunity to reach consensus. This leads to more thoughtful, nuanced policies than the soundbite-driven politics of elections.
  • Restoring Trust: When people see that their neighbors—not career politicians—are making decisions, trust in government increases. A 2020 study found that citizens’ assemblies enjoy higher public approval than elected legislatures because people believe they are more representative and less corrupt.

4. Historical and Modern Precedents for Sortition

Sortition is not a radical, untested idea—it has a long history of success and is already being used in modern democracies.

  • Ancient Athens: The birthplace of democracy relied heavily on sortition. The Boule (council of 500) and many judicial positions were filled by random selection, ensuring that power was distributed among the people rather than concentrated in the hands of elites. Historians credit sortition with preventing corruption and oligarchy in Athens.
  • Venetian Republic (697-1797): Venice used a complex system of sortition and elections to select its leaders, preventing the rise of hereditary aristocracy and maintaining stability for over a thousand years.
  • Modern Citizens’ Assemblies: Countries like Ireland, Canada, the UK, and France have used sortition to tackle contentious issues (abortion, climate change, electoral reform) with great success. In Oregon, a citizens’ assembly helped pass campaign finance reform, proving that sortition can work even in the U.S.

5. Addressing Common Objections to Sortition

Despite its advantages, critics raise several concerns about sortition. However, these objections are either overstated or can be mitigated with careful design.

Objection 1: "Ordinary people aren’t qualified to govern."

  • Response: No one is born knowing how to govern—even elected officials must learn on the job. Sortition-based assemblies provide training, expert testimony, and deliberation time to ensure informed decision-making. Studies show that ordinary citizens, when given the right resources, make better decisions than politicians because they are not constrained by partisan loyalty or donor interests.

Objection 2: "Sortition would lead to chaos and incompetence."

  • Response: Sortition does not mean pure randomness—it can be structured to ensure competence. For example:
    • Stratified sampling ensures diversity (age, gender, race, income, geography).
    • Term limits prevent career politicians.
    • Mentorship programs pair new members with experienced advisors.
    • Hybrid systems (e.g., a randomly selected lower house with an elected upper house) can balance representation and expertise.

Objection 3: "People wouldn’t want to serve."

  • Response: Many people would serve if given the opportunity, especially if compensated fairly. In Ireland’s Citizens’ Assembly, 99% of selected members participated, and many described it as a life-changing experience. Additionally, mandatory short-term service (like jury duty) could be implemented to ensure broad participation.

Objection 4: "Sortition would eliminate accountability."

  • Response: Accountability can be maintained through:
    • Recall mechanisms (citizens can remove corrupt or incompetent members).
    • Transparency requirements (all deliberations are public).
    • Performance reviews (members are evaluated based on their contributions).

Conclusion: A Democratic Revolution

The American electoral system is broken. It has become a tool for the wealthy and well-connected to maintain power while ordinary citizens are left disillusioned and disenfranchised. Sortition offers a radical yet practical solution—one that eliminates corruption, reduces partisanship, and empowers everyday people to shape their own government.

By replacing elections with random selection, the U.S. could: ✅ Eliminate the influence of money in politics by removing the need for fundraising. ✅ Break the two-party stranglehold and encourage consensus-based policymaking. ✅ Create a government that truly represents the people—not just the rich, white, and male. ✅ Restore trust in democracy by proving that ordinary citizens can govern effectively.

The time has come to move beyond elections and embrace a system that is truly democratic—one where every citizen has an equal chance to lead. Sortition is not just an alternative; it is the future of American democracy. The question is not whether we can afford to make this change, but whether we can afford not to.

The idea of sortition—selecting political leaders by random lottery rather than through elections—has gained traction among political theorists, reformers, and some democratic movements as a way to address deep flaws in electoral systems. Advocates argue that a nationwide system of sortition could fundamentally improve fairness, reduce elite influence, and enhance democratic representation in ways that elections cannot. Below is a detailed breakdown of the supposed benefits and reasons for adopting such a system:

1. Eliminating Elite Capture & Reducing Corporate/Political Class Influence

Problem with Elections:

  • Elections favor wealthy, well-connected, and media-savvy candidates, creating a political class that is often disconnected from ordinary citizens.
  • Campaign financing, lobbying, and revolving-door politics mean that elites (corporate, financial, and partisan) dominate policymaking, leading to policies that benefit the few over the many (e.g., tax cuts for the rich, weak financial regulations, corporate subsidies).
  • Incumbency advantage (name recognition, fundraising networks, gerrymandering) makes it nearly impossible for outsiders to win, reinforcing a self-perpetuating elite.

How Sortition Helps:

  • Random selection breaks the power of money and connections. Since anyone can be chosen, there is no need for expensive campaigns, fundraising, or media manipulation.
  • No lobbying or corporate influence on selection. Unlike elected officials who depend on donors, randomly selected citizens have no financial backers to please.
  • Reduces professional politicians. Sortition would replace career politicians with ordinary citizens who serve temporarily, reducing the risk of a permanent political class.
  • Prevents regulatory capture. Since participants are not beholden to special interests, they are more likely to make decisions based on public interest rather than corporate or partisan agendas.

Example:

  • Ancient Athens used sortition for most offices, ensuring that even poor citizens could govern. Modern experiments (e.g., Ireland’s Citizens’ Assembly on abortion, Oregon’s Citizens’ Initiative Review) show that randomly selected groups make thoughtful, evidence-based decisions without elite interference.

2. Enhancing Democratic Representation & Fairness

Problem with Elections:

  • Elections do not produce representative bodies. Wealthy, older, white, male, and highly educated individuals are overrepresented, while women, minorities, young people, and working-class citizens are underrepresented.
  • Voter suppression, gerrymandering, and first-past-the-post systems distort representation, often leading to minority rule (e.g., a party winning a majority of seats with less than 50% of the vote).
  • Low voter turnout (especially among marginalized groups) means that elected officials do not reflect the full diversity of society.

How Sortition Helps:

  • True demographic representation. A well-designed lottery can ensure that the governing body mirrors the population in terms of age, gender, race, income, geography, and education.
  • No gerrymandering or voter suppression. Since selection is random, there is no need for district boundaries or voter registration barriers.
  • Includes marginalized voices. People who never vote (due to disillusionment, lack of time, or systemic barriers) still have a chance to participate.
  • Reduces polarization. Unlike elected politicians who rely on partisan bases, randomly selected citizens are less ideologically extreme and more open to compromise.

Example:

  • A sortition-based legislature could be stratified to ensure proportional representation of all major demographic groups, unlike elections, which often exclude large segments of society.

3. Reducing Corruption & Short-Termism

Problem with Elections:

  • Elected officials are incentivized to prioritize short-term gains (e.g., tax cuts before elections, populist policies) over long-term planning (e.g., climate change, infrastructure, debt reduction).
  • Revolving-door politics (politicians becoming lobbyists) creates conflicts of interest.
  • Partisan gridlock prevents meaningful reform, as politicians fear primary challenges from extremists.

How Sortition Helps:

  • No re-election pressure. Since participants serve fixed terms (e.g., 1-2 years) and cannot be re-selected, they have no incentive to pander to donors or voters—only to make the best decision.
  • Longer-term thinking. Without the need to campaign, participants can focus on evidence-based, sustainable policies rather than short-term political wins.
  • Less partisan extremism. Randomly selected citizens are less ideologically rigid than career politicians, making compromise more likely.
  • Reduced corruption. Since participants are not seeking future office, they are less susceptible to bribes or lobbying.

Example:

  • Climate policy is often stalled by fossil fuel lobbying and short-term electoral cycles. A sortition-based body could make unbiased, long-term decisions without fear of backlash.

4. Increasing Public Trust & Legitimacy

Problem with Elections:

  • Declining trust in government. Many citizens believe elections are rigged, corrupt, or meaningless, leading to apathy, populism, or even democratic backsliding.
  • Perceived illegitimacy. Losing parties often claim fraud (e.g., 2020 U.S. election, Brexit), undermining faith in the system.
  • Low engagement. Many people feel disconnected from politics, believing their vote doesn’t matter.

How Sortition Helps:

  • Perceived fairness. Since selection is random, no one can claim the system is rigged (unlike elections, where gerrymandering, voter suppression, and money in politics create distrust).
  • Greater legitimacy. If the governing body looks like the people, citizens are more likely to accept its decisions.
  • Higher engagement. Knowing that anyone could be selected might encourage more people to stay informed and participate in civic life.
  • Reduces populist demagoguery. Without charismatic leaders rallying bases, extreme rhetoric loses its power, and policy debates become more fact-based.

Example:

  • Iceland’s 2011 constitutional reform used a randomly selected assembly to draft a new constitution, which was widely seen as more legitimate than a traditional political process.

5. Improving Policy Quality & Reducing Partisan Gridlock

Problem with Elections:

  • Partisan polarization leads to government shutdowns, filibusters, and policy paralysis (e.g., U.S. Congress, UK Parliament).
  • Lobbying and special interests distort policy, leading to inefficient or harmful laws (e.g., pharmaceutical price gouging, fossil fuel subsidies).
  • Populist oversimplification. Elected officials often avoid complex solutions (e.g., healthcare, tax reform) to appeal to voters.

How Sortition Helps:

  • Deliberative decision-making. Randomly selected citizens can study issues in depth, hear from experts, and debate without partisan pressure.
  • Less ideological extremism. Unlike politicians who cater to bases, sortition participants are more open to evidence and compromise.
  • Better long-term planning. Without election cycles, they can focus on what works rather than what polls well.
  • Reduced influence of misinformation. Unlike elected officials who spread partisan narratives, sortition bodies can fact-check and deliberate before deciding.

Example:

  • Canada’s Citizens’ Assembly on Electoral Reform (2004) recommended a new voting system after months of study, showing that ordinary citizens can make complex policy decisions when given the time and resources.

6. Reducing the Cost of Politics

Problem with Elections:

  • Campaigns are expensive. In the U.S., presidential elections cost billions, and congressional races are increasingly unaffordable for non-wealthy candidates.
  • Fundraising takes time. Politicians spend 30-70% of their time fundraising, distracting from governance.
  • Corporate and wealthy donors expect favors in return, leading to legalized corruption.

How Sortition Helps:

  • No campaigns = no fundraising. Sortition eliminates the need for expensive ads, consultants, and rallies.
  • No need for political parties. Since selection is random, parties lose their gatekeeping power, reducing their influence over policy.
  • Lower barriers to entry. Anyone can be selected, regardless of wealth or connections.

Example:

  • Ancient Athens had no campaign costs because officials were chosen by lot. Modern sortition experiments (e.g., Ireland’s Citizens’ Assembly) operate at a fraction of the cost of elections.

Potential Challenges & Criticisms of Sortition

While sortition has many advantages, it is not without potential drawbacks:

  1. Lack of Expertise – Randomly selected citizens may lack knowledge of complex issues (though this can be mitigated with training, expert briefings, and deliberation).
  2. Accountability Issues – Since participants are not elected, they cannot be voted out, raising concerns about unaccountable power (though fixed terms and recall mechanisms could address this).
  3. Public Skepticism – Many people are unfamiliar with sortition and may distrust a system that doesn’t involve voting.
  4. Implementation Complexity – Designing a fair, stratified lottery that ensures diversity without manipulation is challenging.
  5. Resistance from Elites – Politicians, parties, and lobbyists would fiercely oppose a system that removes their power.

How a Nationwide Sortition System Might Work

A hybrid model (combining sortition with elections) could be a practical first step:

  1. Legislature:
    • One chamber (e.g., House of Representatives) selected by sortition, stratified to represent the population.
    • The other chamber (e.g., Senate) elected traditionally (to maintain some accountability).
    • Fixed terms (1-2 years) with no re-selection to prevent careerism.
  2. Executive Branch:
    • President/Prime Minister chosen by a randomly selected electoral college (rather than popular vote or partisan electors).
    • Or, a small executive council selected by lot (like Switzerland’s Federal Council).
  3. Judiciary & Independent Bodies:
    • Supreme Court justices or regulatory commissioners could be selected by sortition from a pool of qualified candidates.
  4. Citizens’ Assemblies for Major Decisions:
    • Randomly selected bodies could be convened for constitutional amendments, major reforms, or contentious issues (e.g., climate policy, healthcare).

Conclusion: Why Sortition Could Be a Democratic Revolution

Sortition offers a radical but practical alternative to elections, addressing many of the deepest flaws in modern democracy: ✅ Breaks elite control by removing money and connections from politics. ✅ Ensures true representation by including all demographics, not just the wealthy and well-connected. ✅ Reduces corruption and short-termism by eliminating re-election incentives. ✅ Increases public trust by making government more transparent and fair. ✅ Improves policy quality through deliberation rather than partisan posturing.

While not a perfect system, sortition could complement or even replace elections in a way that makes democracy more inclusive, fair, and effective. The biggest hurdle is political will—elites who benefit from the current system would resist it, but growing public disillusionment with elections may create an opening for reform.

Would you support a system where your neighbor, rather than a career politician, could end up making laws? For many, the answer is yes.

Elections, as currently practiced, are structurally corrupt. The system is not merely marred by isolated scandals but is designed to generate corruption. Rethinking Democracy: The Case for Sortition

A Note on This Essay

The following presents strong arguments favoring sortition—not necessarily an endorsement that it's superior. I'll also address major counterarguments at the end. A complete analysis requires wrestling with both.

Introduction

The American electoral system is broken. Campaign finance has transformed politicians into fundraisers. Gerrymandering ensures predetermined outcomes. Tribal partisanship has made compromise impossible. Rather than reform around the margins, we should consider a radical alternative: sortition—selecting legislative and executive officials through random citizen selection, like jury duty.

This isn't utopian fantasy. Ancient Athens used it for most offices. The Belgian system has experimented with it. Randomly selected citizen assemblies increasingly inform policy worldwide. While unconventional, sortition addresses fundamental flaws in competitive elections.

The Corruption Problem Elections Create

Elections demand resources. Candidates need millions to win visible office. This reality naturally filters who runs: the wealthy, the connected, those willing to owe favors to donors.

Money hasn't just corrupted elections—it has defined them. A 2014 Princeton study found Congress responds to wealthy donors' preferences, not median voters'. Sortition eliminates this dynamic entirely. Random citizens selected from across income levels owe nothing to anyone before taking office.

Campaign funding disappears as an issue. No one fundraises for a lottery. This alone removes a primary corruption vector.

Partisanship as a Design Flaw

The electoral system produces tribalism structurally:

  • Primary elections reward appeals to base voters, pushing candidates to ideological extremes
  • Reelection pressure forces constant campaigning, preventing careful deliberation
  • Team loyalty becomes necessary for fundraising and organizational support
  • Winnable districts (through gerrymandering) mean representatives answer to narrow parties, not constituents

A legislature composed of randomly selected ordinary citizens lacks these incentives. They didn't build careers in partisan structures. They have no reelection campaign. They weren't funded by ideological donors.

Research on citizen assemblies (the closest real-world model) shows participants converge toward pragmatic compromise. When people aren't performing for media or donors, and when they speak with peers representing different viewpoints, ideological rigidity softens. Citizens prioritize actual problem-solving over scoring points.

Democratic Legitimacy Reconsidered

We assume elections = democracy. But elections actually represent only one interpretation of democratic values.

Democracy means: power resides with the people.

Elections achieve this through a delegating model: we choose representatives who exercise power on our behalf.

Sortition achieves this through a participation model: ordinary people directly exercise power as representatives. The legislator isn't a specially trained politician—they're you, or your neighbor.

This is arguably more democratic. In 2024, trust in Congress is at historic lows (10-20% approval). Not because Congress lacks elections, but because elections filter for professional politicians disconnected from ordinary life.

A randomly selected legislature would literally be the people. A nurse, a small business owner, a teacher, a truck driver, a retired social worker. They know their peers' actual concerns—childcare costs, healthcare access, job instability—through lived experience, not polling.

Reducing Elite Capture

Professional politicians form a distinct class:

  • They spend careers in politics or closely related fields
  • They network within political circles
  • Their interests (secure seats, higher office) diverge from constituents'
  • Deep-pocketed interests court this class intensively

Sortition floods the legislature with people whose primary interests lie elsewhere. A randomly selected engineer doesn't want permanent office—they want to solve genuine problems, then return to engineering. They're harder to coopt because they're not building a political career.

This also means the position can't be promised to allies or inherited. The mayor's brother can't leverage connections into a legislative seat. This removes entire pathways of elite privilege.

Practical Advantages

Reduced campaign polarization: No campaign season means 18 months of divisive rhetoric every two years isn't inevitable.

Better deliberation: Citizens on assemblies spend months studying issues. They outperform many legislatures in understanding complex policy trade-offs.

Diverse representation: Random selection produces demographic representation far better than elections, which privilege wealthy candidates who can afford campaigns.

Professionalism: Participants receive training, support staff, and time to do the work properly—not squeezing it between fundraising calls.

Major Counterarguments Worth Considering

Before concluding, the strongest objections:

Competence: Do random citizens possess sufficient knowledge? Citizens do outperform expectations on assemblies, but governing a nation differs from voting on a local issue. This requires serious institutional design (strong support staff, extended deliberation periods, preventing demagogues).

Accountability: Elections create accountability—bad representatives can be removed. Randomly selected legislators can't be recalled. Sortition requires different accountability mechanisms (transparency, term limits, performance reviews), which are harder to implement.

Motivation: Why would people accept jury-like conscription to legislative service? What prevents shirking? Elections motivate through ambition; sortition must motivate through civic duty—a weaker force.

Stability: Constant turnover and inexperience could produce impulsive policy. Continuous change might prevent coherent long-term governance.

Coordination: A diverse legislature without party discipline might fail to coordinate on major projects.

These aren't fatal, but they're real. Sortition requires institutional safeguards elections currently provide.

Conclusion

The American electoral system reliably produces: politicians beholden to donors, tribal partisanship, gerrymandered safe seats, and public distrust. Incremental reform has failed repeatedly.

Sortition offers a genuinely different path. It removes corruption incentives, reduces partisanship causes, enables genuine citizen power, and filters out professional political interests. It's not perfect—nothing is—but it addresses real pathologies that competitive elections structurally embed.

We've tried elections for 240 years. Perhaps it's worth seriously examining alternatives, not as fantasy, but as systems with historical precedent and growing empirical validation from citizen assembly experiments.

Democracy should mean the people govern. Sortition means that more directly than elections ever could.

Democracy Reimagined: Why the United States Should Replace Elections with Sortition

For over two centuries, the United States has prided itself on its system of representative democracy, grounded in free and fair elections. Yet, today, American democracy faces a crisis of legitimacy, efficacy, and trust. Public confidence in political institutions is at historic lows. Political polarization has reached fever pitch, governance is gridlocked, and a sense of alienation permeates the electorate. The solution to this systemic decay lies not in reforming elections, but in reimagining them entirely—by replacing elections with sortition, a system in which legislative and executive leaders are selected at random from the citizenry, mirroring the democratic principles of ancient Athens combined with modern civic engagement. The time has come for the United States to embrace sortition as the cornerstone of a truly representative, equitable, and functional democracy.

1. Sortition Removes Political Corruption at Its Root

Corruption in American politics is not a bug—it is a feature of a system that relies on fundraising, lobbying, and electoral competition. Elections incentivize money: candidates must raise millions, often from wealthy donors and special interests, to win. The result? A quid pro quo political culture where access, influence, and policy outcomes are openly traded for campaign contributions. According to the Center for Responsive Politics, the 2020 U.S. elections cost over $14 billion, most of it funneled into advertising and outreach, not governance.

Sortition dismantles this machinery of corruption. When officials are selected at random, there is no campaign finance apparatus to sustain. Randomly selected citizens have no incentives to curry favor with donors, no need to attend fundraising dinners, and no obligation to special interests. As historian and democratic theorist David Van Reybrouck puts it, "Sortition removes the very possibility of buying power."

Moreover, selection by lottery ensures a broadly representative political class. Unlike in elections, where candidates often emerge from elite institutions (law schools, corporate boardrooms, or political dynasties), a sortition-based system draws from all walks of life: teachers, plumbers, truck drivers, gig workers, retirees, and college students. This diversity of lived experience insulates governance from the narrow, self-serving agendas of political insiders and makes corruption far harder to organize or sustain.

2. Sortition Drastically Reduces Partisanship and Political Polarization

The United States suffers from a deep and growing partisan divide, exacerbated by a winner-take-all electoral system. Elections incentivize ideological extremism: candidates appeal to their base, not the center, to survive primaries and win general elections. The media ecosystem rewards outrage, politicians gain prominence by being combative, and compromise is seen as betrayal.

Sortition, by contrast, selects leaders through random sampling, not ambition. Most people drawn through sortition will have no prior political affiliation, career ambitions, or tribal loyalties. The process is designed to produce a truly deliberative microcosm of society—a group of citizens who reflect the nation’s geographic, economic, racial, and social diversity.

This "mirror representation" shifts the focus from partisan rhetoric to deliberative democracy. Drawing from the success of citizen assemblies in Ireland, France, and Canada—where randomly selected citizens have debated and shaped landmark policies on climate change and abortion—evidence shows that such bodies are more likely to engage in good-faith dialogue, seek compromise, and focus on long-term solutions, not short-term political gains.

Because participants are not running for reelection or beholden to party leadership, they are freer to change their minds, support bipartisan solutions, vote against party lines, and even cross ideological divides. When 150–500 randomly selected citizens deliberate together, guided by expert testimony, moderators, and clear agendas, they develop a collective intelligence that transcends the ideological gridlock of Congress. The result? Policies grounded in evidence, public interest, and common sense—not fear, fundraising, or party loyalty.

3. Sortition Empowers Ordinary People and Reclaims Democratic Agency

Elections—especially in the U.S.—reinforce a top-down model of governance that disempowers the masses. Only 1–2% of the population votes in primaries, and even fewer contribute financially. The average citizen feels irrelevant, cynical, and alienated, believing that their vote “doesn’t matter” or that the system is “rigged.” This erosion of civic agency is one of the most corrosive forces in modern democracy.

Sortition reverses this dynamic. It says: every citizen is equally capable of, and entitled to, political leadership. When 500 Americans are selected at random to serve as lawmakers, it sends a powerful message: You matter. Your voice, your experience, your perspective belong in the halls of power.

This is not merely symbolic. Empirical studies show that participating in a citizen assembly boosts political efficacy, trust in institutions, and civic engagement long after the term ends. People who serve gain political literacy, pride in their contributions, and a renewed belief in the possibility of collective action. In France’s 2021 Climate Assembly, 97% of participants reported feeling proud of their work, and 60% committed to continuing civic activism in their communities.

Furthermore, sortition democratizes leadership. It bypasses the need for political experience or charisma—qualities often valued over wisdom or integrity. A former teacher, a retail worker, or a nurse can sit at the table as equals with lawyers and engineers. The system does not reward the loudest, the most charismatic, or the best dresser, but the most thoughtful, the most empathetic, and the most willing to listen.

4. A Practical Framework for Implementation: Phasing In Sortition

Skeptics may question the feasibility of replacing elections. But sortition does not require an overnight revolution. A phased, parallel approach can ensure stability and public buy-in:

  1. Establish a National Citizens’ Assembly (NCA): A standing body of 300–500 citizens, randomly selected every two years, would begin by issuing non-binding recommendations on complex issues (e.g., climate policy, AI regulation, healthcare reform). This builds legitimacy and incorporates sortition in advisory roles.

  2. Adopt a Sortition-Based Lower House: The House of Representatives could gradually transition: 50% elected, 50% selected by lot. Over time, the proportion increases. This mirrors the “hybrid democracy” model proposed by democratic innovators like Brett Hennig.

  3. Appoint Ministers and Committee Chairs via Sortition: Executive leadership could be drawn from the NCA or a separate panel, combining expertise with democratic legitimacy. The President could remain elected, but cabinet appointments—especially for policy-intensive roles—could be selected randomly from pre-vetted citizens.

  4. Train and Support Participants: Randomly selected citizens receive training in governance, media literacy, and conflict resolution. They are paid a living wage, given housing near Congress, and shielded from harassment. This ensures that participation is accessible and dignified.

  5. Use Technology for Transparency: All deliberations would be streamed live, archived, and subjected to public commentary. Real-time fact-checking and expert panels ensure accuracy and accountability.

5. Addressing Objections: Sortition Is Not “Rule by Lottery”—It’s Rule by Microcosm

Critics often argue that sortition would lead to incompetence—“random people making random decisions.” But this misunderstands how modern sortition works. Unlike in early Athenian democracy, today’s citizen assemblies are structured, informed, and supported. Participants hear from experts, civil society groups, and stakeholders. They deliberate over weeks or months, not minutes. They receive facilitation, procedural guidance, and fact-checking.

Moreover, diversity enhances decision-making. Cognitive science tells us that diverse groups outperform homogeneous, “expert-only” bodies in complex, high-stakes environments. A randomly selected body is more likely to include someone who has experienced housing insecurity, rural broadband deserts, or the opioid crisis—perspectives missing from Washington.

Others argue that sortition weakens accountability. But election-based accountability is already broken. Constituents rarely punish representatives for harmful votes; instead, voters often re-elect failed leaders due to party loyalty. Sortition introduces a new kind of accountability: transparency, public deliberation, and community oversight. A citizen who serves for a term remains embedded in their community, ensuring lived experience guides future engagement.

Conclusion: A Democracy Worthy of the People

The United States stands at a crossroads. We can continue recycling the same broken patterns—spending billions on campaigns, rewarding division, and producing governance without popular legitimacy. Or we can choose a bolder, more authentic path: a democracy where power flows from the people, not party machines; where decisions are made by informed, diverse, and ordinary citizens; where integrity is rewarded over ambition.

Sortition is not a betrayal of democracy—it is its purification. It removes the corruptive influence of money and power. It heals the wounds of polarization by fostering dialogue over division. It restores agency to the 99.9% of Americans who have never held public office but whose lives are shaped by it.

This is not utopian fantasy. It is happening—in Ireland, in Melbourne, in Weymouth, and in countless community-driven initiatives around the world. The United States, as the self-proclaimed beacon of democracy, has a moral and practical imperative to lead this transformation.

Let us replace the circus of elections with the quiet, profound power of random selection. Let us choose not candidates, but citizens. Let us build a government that truly reflects we the people. In doing so, we will not merely revitalize democracy—we will fulfill it.

It is time to put the future in the hands of the people, by the luck of the draw.
