The Lottery of Liberty: Why America Should Replace Elections with Sortition

I. The Machine Is Not Broken — It Is Working Exactly as Designed

Americans have been told for two centuries that elections are the beating heart of democracy. Yet consider what our elections actually produce. Congress routinely earns approval ratings below 25 percent, and yet more than 90 percent of House incumbents who seek reelection win. Campaign spending in a single federal cycle now exceeds $14 billion. Roughly $4 billion a year flows into federal lobbying. Landmark research by political scientists Martin Gilens and Benjamin Page found that when the preferences of average citizens diverge from those of economic elites and organized business interests, the average citizen's independent influence on policy outcomes is statistically close to zero.

This is not a system that has failed. It is a system that has succeeded at something other than representing the people. Elections do not select for wisdom, integrity, or public-spiritedness. They select for the ability to win elections — which means the ability to raise money, cultivate donors, dominate media cycles, and please the small, ideologically extreme slice of the electorate that votes in primaries. We then express shock when the people who are extraordinarily good at those things turn out to be mediocre at governing.

The reform movement has spent a century tinkering: campaign finance limits, disclosure rules, independent redistricting, ranked-choice voting, term limits. Each is a patch on a hull that is structurally unsound. The problem is not that our elections are corrupted. The problem is that elections, by their nature, generate the incentives that corruption feeds on. If we want government by and for ordinary people, we should stop asking who can best win a popularity contest and instead do what democracy's inventors did: draw lots.

II. Sortition Is Not a Thought Experiment

Sortition — the selection of officeholders by lottery from among the citizenry — is the oldest democratic technology we have. In classical Athens, the Council of Five Hundred, the juries, and most magistracies were filled by lot. Aristotle stated the principle without ambiguity: selection by lot is characteristic of democracy, while election is characteristic of oligarchy. The Athenians understood that if only the ambitious, the eloquent, and the wealthy can obtain office, then only they will be governed for. Renaissance Venice and Florence used lotteries to blunt factional capture. And Americans use sortition every single day: we entrust randomly selected citizens with the power to strip a fellow citizen of liberty, property, and — in some states — life itself. We call this a jury, and we consider it a bulwark of freedom.

Nor is sortition confined to history. Over the past two decades, governments have convened hundreds of randomly selected citizens' assemblies. The OECD has catalogued nearly 300 such bodies across dozens of countries. British Columbia's Citizens' Assembly on Electoral Reform (2004) produced a sophisticated proposal after a year of study by 160 randomly chosen residents. Ireland's Constitutional Convention and Citizens' Assembly — ordinary people, farmers and nurses and retirees, selected by lot — did what a paralyzed political class could not: they deliberated calmly on same-sex marriage and abortion, two of the most explosive questions in Irish life, and produced recommendations that the electorate then ratified by referendum. The German-speaking community of Belgium has established a permanent, sortition-based Citizens' Council. Stanford's Deliberative Polling experiments, including the 2019 "America in One Room" gathering, repeatedly show that when a representative random sample of Americans is given good information, expert testimony, and time to talk, polarization decreases and policy views converge toward considered judgment.

The evidence is in. Ordinary citizens, properly resourced, deliberate well. The question is why we confine them to advisory roles while leaving real power in the hands of a professional political class that no one respects.

III. Sortition Eliminates the Root of Political Corruption

Corruption in America is largely legal, and that is precisely the problem. No one hands a senator a briefcase of cash. Instead, a system of mutual dependency operates in plain sight: a legislator needs millions of dollars to survive the next cycle; industries and interest groups have millions; access, attention, and legislative language flow in one direction while money flows in the other. Members of Congress have described devoting hours of every workday to "call time" — dialing donors instead of studying bills. Roughly half of departing members find work in the influence industry, where their value is measured in relationships purchased at public expense.

Sortition severs every link in this chain at once.

There is no campaign, so there is no campaign finance. A citizen selected by lot does not fundraise, does not court bundlers, does not owe anyone a hearing. The single largest vector of moneyed influence in American politics simply ceases to exist — not regulated, not disclosed, but structurally impossible.

There is no reelection, so there is no permanent electoral debt. With single, non-renewable terms, a legislator's decisions cannot be leveraged against her future. She cannot be threatened with a primary challenge funded by a slighted industry. She cannot be rewarded with an independent expenditure campaign. The threat and the bribe both lose their grip, because there is no future candidacy to threaten or reward.

There is no party apparatus to capture. Today, an interest group that wants influence need not persuade 535 people; it can concentrate resources on party leadership, committee chairs, and the small number of competitive districts that determine control. In a sortition legislature, power is dispersed among hundreds of independent citizens with no shared career interest, no whip, and no leadership hierarchy to bend. Capturing such a body would require corrupting hundreds of unpredictable strangers who did not seek office, cannot keep it, and rotate out on a schedule.

The revolving door can be nailed shut. Because sortition service is a temporary civic duty rather than a career rung, cooling-off periods and lifetime lobbying bans impose no professional hardship. A randomly selected schoolteacher returns to teaching. She has no incentive to spend her term auditioning for a $500,000 job at a trade association.

Elections require us to trust that people whose survival depends on donors will ignore donors. Sortition simply removes the donors.

IV. Sortition Dissolves Toxic Partisanship

American political dysfunction is not caused primarily by disagreement — free people will always disagree. It is caused by institutionalized disagreement: a machinery that converts ordinary pluralism into permanent tribal warfare because warfare wins elections.

The mechanisms are well understood. Gerrymandering and geographic sorting have reduced genuinely competitive House districts to a small fraction of the total, meaning most legislators face no general-election threat and only a primary threat — and primaries are dominated by the most ideologically committed voters. The rational strategy is not persuasion but purity. Compromise becomes betrayal. Meanwhile, negative partisanship — the mobilizing power of loathing the other side — makes conflict more electorally profitable than achievement. A bill that solves a problem denies your opponents a grievance and your base a villain. Legislators therefore have structural reasons to prefer stalemate.

Sortition removes every one of these incentives.

A randomly selected chamber has no districts to gerrymander, because it has no districts. It has no primaries, because there are no candidates. It has no party discipline, because parties exist to win elections, and there are no elections to win. A citizen legislator does not need to demonize a colleague to secure her seat; she does not need a fundraising villain; she gains nothing from a shutdown. She has one term to accomplish something and then must return to the community that will live with the results.

This is not naïve optimism; it is the consistent empirical finding of deliberative bodies. Random samples of citizens, placed in rooms with good information and facilitation and a task to complete, behave dramatically differently from partisans in front of cameras. Participants in citizens' assemblies routinely report changed minds, reduced hostility toward opponents, and surprise at how much common ground existed beneath the noise. The partisanship we mistake for the American character is largely an artifact of the incentives we impose on our representatives — and of a media ecosystem that covers politics as a permanent campaign. Remove the campaign and much of the venom has nothing to feed on.

A sortition legislature would still contain conservatives and progressives, and it should. But it would contain them as citizens reasoning, not as soldiers in a war for institutional control.

V. Sortition Actually Empowers Ordinary People

Here is the quiet scandal of representative government: our representatives do not resemble us and never have. Congress is disproportionately composed of lawyers, businesspeople, and the wealthy; a majority of its members have long been millionaires, in a country where the median household holds a small fraction of that in net worth. Working-class Americans — the roughly half of the labor force in manual, service, and clerical jobs — are almost entirely absent. Political scientist Nicholas Carnes has shown that this class gap is not cosmetic: legislators from working-class backgrounds vote measurably differently on economic policy. When no one in the room has ever worried about rent, eviction policy is discussed in the abstract.

Sortition fixes this by construction, not aspiration. A stratified random sample of the American people is the American people: nurses, welders, truck drivers, small business owners, veterans, caregivers, farmers, adjuncts, retirees. It includes rural voices without needing a Senate, and minority voices without needing a lawsuit. No campaign consultant decides who is "electable." No donor network filters the pool. No one is excluded for lacking charisma, wealth, a clean social media history, or the peculiar psychology that drives a person to spend years asking strangers for money.

That last point deserves emphasis. Elections do not select randomly from among the competent; they select for ambition. They systematically advantage the self-promoting over the self-effacing, the certain over the thoughtful, the person who wants power over the person who would use it well. Sortition is the only selection method that does not filter for the desire to rule. Plato's ancient worry — that those who seek office are the least fit to hold it — finds its only practical answer in the lottery.

And critically, sortition transforms citizenship itself. Under elections, the citizen's role is reduced to a few minutes in a booth every other November, choosing between options assembled by others. Under sortition, every adult carries a real possibility of governing, and every governing body is filled with people the rest of us actually know: our neighbors, coworkers, relatives. Political power stops being something done to us by a distant caste and becomes a civic obligation shared across the population, like jury duty. That is what "consent of the governed" was supposed to mean.

VI. How It Would Actually Work

Sortition is a design problem, and the design work has largely been done by scholars such as Bernard Manin, David Van Reybrouck, Hélène Landemore, and Alexander Guerrero.

Selection. A stratified random sample drawn from the full adult population, weighted to match the nation on age, sex, race, education, income, geography, and region — a much stronger guarantee of demographic representativeness than any election has ever delivered. Serving is compensated generously (a professional salary, childcare, housing, job protection, and reintegration support), so that service is a genuine opportunity rather than a burden only the comfortable can bear.

Structure. A large legislature — several hundred members, large enough to be statistically representative — with staggered, non-renewable terms of three to four years, so that experienced members always mentor incoming ones and the body never resets wholesale. Executive functions are directed by a smaller randomly selected council, supported by a professional, politically neutral civil service and agency heads it appoints and can dismiss.

Support. Members receive intensive onboarding, nonpartisan analytic staff (an expanded CBO and CRS model), professional facilitation, and mandated hearings that present competing expert views rather than one-sided testimony. Deliberation happens in small working groups before plenary decisions — the format that empirical research shows produces the highest-quality citizen judgment.

Accountability. Multiple independent randomly selected bodies check one another: a policy chamber, a separate oversight chamber that audits implementation, and an ethics tribunal with real subpoena and removal power. Full transparency of records and finances, aggressive conflict-of-interest rules, and criminal penalties for influence-peddling. Add a citizen-initiated referendum as a final popular veto, and the public retains a direct check that today's voters, choosing between two pre-approved brands, do not actually possess.

VII. Answering the Objections

"Ordinary people aren't qualified." Neither are most legislators; the median member of Congress is not an economist, epidemiologist, or engineer either. What legislators do is evaluate competing expert claims and make value judgments about tradeoffs. Value judgments are precisely what citizens are qualified to make — and on the analytic side, a random sample brings a broader range of real-world knowledge than a chamber of lawyers. We already trust juries to master forensic evidence in complex trials. We trust them because we know that ordinary people, given time, information, and responsibility, rise to it. Every citizens' assembly on record confirms it.

"There's no accountability without elections." Elections are a remarkably weak accountability mechanism: one blunt, retrospective, bundled judgment every few years, in races where over 90 percent of incumbents win, most districts are uncompetitive, and voters cannot punish a specific betrayal without also discarding everything else. Sortition replaces this fiction with stronger tools: mandatory rotation (guaranteed turnover, not hoped-for turnover), transparency, independent audit chambers, judicial review, referendum, and — most powerfully — the fact that every legislator returns to ordinary life under the laws she wrote. That is skin in the game elections cannot provide.

"It would be illegitimate — no one voted for them." Legitimacy comes from procedures the public recognizes as fair and from outcomes the public recognizes as responsive. Random selection is the fairest imaginable allocation of a scarce office: it gives every citizen an equal chance, which is a stronger equality than one vote among a hundred million. Polls of citizens' assembly outcomes and referendum ratification in Ireland and elsewhere suggest publics accept — often prefer — decisions made by "people like us" over decisions made by politicians they distrust.

"Interest groups would manipulate naïve amateurs." Manipulation is far easier under the current system, where lobbyists cultivate the same members for decades and write bill text outright. Sortition presents influence-seekers with a nightmare: hundreds of unpredictable, unknown, non-repeating decision-makers, protected by professional staff, adversarial hearings, and transparency rules, none of whom needs money or a future job. The real risk — capture by permanent staff — is a serious design challenge, addressed by rotating staff, competing analytic sources, staggered member terms, and independent oversight chambers. It is a manageable problem; systemic donor dependency is not.

VIII. Conclusion: Democracy Without Politicians

We have confused a means with an end. Elections were adopted not because they maximized democracy but because, in the eighteenth century, they were the practical way to constitute a government across a vast territory — and, candidly, because many framers wanted a filter that would keep power in the hands of "the better sort." We inherited that filter and then spent two centuries insisting it was the essence of self-rule.

It is not. Self-rule means that the people govern. Today the people choose, from a menu written by donors and party gatekeepers, which member of a distant professional class will govern them — and then watch that class perform conflict for the cameras while wealth writes the substance of policy. Americans sense this. Trust in government sits near historic lows, and majorities in both parties believe the system is rigged. They are not paranoid. They are describing the incentive structure accurately.

Sortition offers something elections cannot: a legislature with no donors, no primaries, no gerrymanders, no reelection campaigns, no party whips, and no career politicians — filled instead with a genuine cross-section of the American people, given the time, information, and support to reason together about the country's future, and then sent home to live under the laws they made.

We already trust random citizens with a person's liberty and life. It is time to trust them with the republic. Draw the lots.

Serious counterarguments exist — concerning democratic legitimacy without consent through voting, the accountability functions elections perform, the risk of staff and expert capture, and the enormous constitutional obstacles to such a change — and a full assessment would weigh them in more depth than a persuasive essay permits.

The Case for Sortition

Sortition—filling public offices by lottery from the citizenry rather than by election—is one of the oldest ideas in democratic theory and one of the most actively debated reforms today. Below is the case its advocates make, followed by a brief note on the main objections, since understanding the strongest counterarguments is part of understanding the proposal.

The historical and theoretical foundation

Sortition is not a novelty. Classical Athens filled its 500-member Council, its juries, and most magistracies by lot, reserving election mainly for generals. Aristotle treated the distinction as definitional: "the appointment of magistrates by lot is thought to be democratic, and the election of them oligarchic." Renaissance Venice and Florence used lotteries extensively to prevent factional capture. Montesquieu, Harrington, and Guicciardini all discussed the lot as a republican safeguard.

Advocates argue that the 18th-century shift to purely electoral government was, in part, a deliberate choice by elites—Madison's hope for representatives who would "refine and enlarge the public views"—rather than a discovery that elections are more democratic. Bernard Manin's influential history frames modern representative government as a distinct regime type, not democracy's natural form.

Statistical representativeness

The core argument is descriptive: a sufficiently large random sample resembles the population it is drawn from. A 500-person allotted chamber would automatically approximate the public's distribution of income, occupation, education, age, gender, race, region, disability, religion, and life experience—without quotas or identity-based districting.

Elected legislatures do not. Legislators are overwhelmingly drawn from law, business, and professional occupations; working-class representation in most Western legislatures has collapsed to a few percent, even as roughly half the population works in manual, service, or clerical jobs. Nicholas Carnes's research suggests this matters substantively: legislators of working-class origin vote differently on economic issues than their affluent colleagues, controlling for party and district. If descriptive absence produces substantive distortion, a lottery corrects it mechanically.

Removing money from the selection process

Sortition eliminates campaigns, and with them the "wealth primary." There are no donors to court, no fundraising calls, no independent expenditures, no advertising arms race, no incentive to shape policy in anticipation of a future donation. This addresses what critics see as the central corruption of contemporary democracies not by regulating money in politics but by removing the mechanism through which money enters.

Lobbying also becomes structurally harder. Sustained influence depends on stable relationships with identifiable, durable decision-makers—committee chairs, whips, leadership. A body whose members are unpredictable, non-renewable, and rotating offers no such purchase. The Athenians understood this: juries were allotted the same morning to prevent bribery. Advocates add that the "revolving door" weakens too, since allotted members have no political career to protect or monetize in the same way.

Escaping electoral incentives

Elections create re-election incentives, and advocates argue those incentives systematically distort governance:

  • Short-termism. Costs beyond the next election cycle—climate adaptation, pension solvency, infrastructure, pandemic preparedness—are chronically underweighted. A body facing no re-election can, in principle, weigh long horizons neutrally.
  • Position-taking over problem-solving. Elected politicians are rewarded for visible credit-claiming and blame-avoidance rather than for quiet effective policy.
  • Rigidity. Politicians cannot change their minds without being accused of flip-flopping. Participants in citizens' assemblies routinely shift views as evidence accumulates, precisely because nothing punishes them for it.
  • Partisan sabotage. Where one party's success is another's electoral loss, obstruction becomes rational. Without parties or re-election, that logic disappears.

Adverse selection in elections

A subtler argument: elections don't select for governing ability, they select for campaign-winning ability. The traits that win campaigns—charisma, relentless self-promotion, comfort with strategic ambiguity, appetite for conflict, tolerance for fundraising, extreme ambition—are at best orthogonal and at worst inversely related to judiciousness, humility, and public-spiritedness. Sortition doesn't select for competence either, but proponents argue that a random draw at least doesn't select against the relevant virtues. It also structurally excludes demagogues: there is no campaign to win by inflaming a public.

Political equality as equal chance to rule

Elections give citizens equal votes but wildly unequal prospects of holding office. Sortition realizes what the Greeks called isonomia and Aristotle's ideal of "ruling and being ruled in turn": every citizen has an equal, non-zero chance of actual power. It also implicitly enfranchises the politically disengaged—non-voters, the alienated, those who believe the system ignores them—who appear in the sample in proportion to their numbers.

Structural immunity to electoral pathologies

With no elections, there is nothing to gerrymander, no voter rolls to purge, no ballots to contest, no turnout to suppress, no election-day disinformation, no foreign interference in campaigns, no doubt about certified results. A whole class of democratic crises simply has no attack surface.

Deliberative quality and epistemic diversity

Empirical experience with deliberative mini-publics is the strongest evidence base advocates cite. Ireland's Citizens' Assembly produced the recommendations that led to the same-sex marriage and abortion referendums, resolving issues the party system had avoided for decades. British Columbia's Citizens' Assembly on Electoral Reform, Belgium's permanent Ostbelgien Citizens' Council, France's Convention Citoyenne pour le Climat, and hundreds of OECD-catalogued cases suggest that ordinary people, given time, balanced briefings, adversarial expert testimony, and skilled facilitation, produce coherent and often courageous recommendations.

Theoretically, Hong and Page's work on cognitive diversity suggests that heterogeneous groups can outperform homogeneous expert groups on complex problems—random selection maximizes such diversity, whereas elections and professional recruitment homogenize.

Legitimacy and civic effects

Surveys often find citizens report more trust in decisions made by "people like me" than by politicians. And mass participation would be transformative in scale: in a country of 300 million with rotating allotted bodies, millions would eventually serve, and tens of millions would know someone who had. Research on jury service finds it durably increases subsequent civic participation—an effect that could compound society-wide.

How proponents propose to make it workable

Serious designs are more elaborate than "one random chamber":

  • Stratified sampling and large bodies (hundreds to thousands) to control sampling error.
  • Generous compensation, job protection, childcare, and accessibility support, so service isn't restricted to those who can afford it—critical because opt-outs otherwise bias the sample toward the leisured and confident.
  • Functional separation, as in Terrill Bouricius's multi-body model: separate allotted bodies for agenda-setting, policy drafting, review, final voting (by secret ballot to resist pressure), and oversight—so no single group holds unchecked power.
  • Rotation and staggered terms for continuity plus turnover.
  • Professional but neutral support: nonpartisan staff, adversarial expert panels, trained facilitators, transparency requirements.
  • Accountability reconceived as ex ante representativeness plus ex post audit—modeled on the Athenian euthyna—along with judicial review, constitutional constraints, and in some designs referendums or a retained elected chamber as a check.
  • The executive, harder to allot, is usually handled indirectly: allotted councils appoint, oversee, and can remove professional executives, or an allotted body confirms senior officials.

Most contemporary advocates propose hybrid systems—an allotted second chamber, an allotted body with agenda or veto power, sortition for constitutional questions—rather than wholesale replacement.

The serious objections

Honesty requires noting these, because they are the crux of the scholarly debate:

  • Competence and experience in complex domains like macroeconomics, defense, and law.
  • Accountability. Voters can throw out bad governments; there is no comparable sanction on a lottery-selected body, and no way for the public to signal "we want a different direction."
  • Capture shifts rather than disappears. Amateur decision-makers may depend heavily on staff, agenda-setters, expert witnesses, and facilitators—who are unelected and unallotted. Influence-seekers would target these chokepoints.
  • No mandates or programmatic coherence, and no mechanism for citizens to choose between rival visions of the future.
  • Consent. Being governed by people you had no hand in choosing strikes many as a different kind of legitimacy deficit—and compelling unwilling citizens to govern raises its own problems.
  • Minority protection. Parties, for all their faults, build cross-cutting coalitions; a body reflecting raw majority sentiment may be less protective of unpopular minorities. Strong constitutional limits become essential.
  • Sampling risk. Any single draw could be unrepresentative, and small margins on major decisions would rest on the accident of who was picked.
  • Transition and stability. Replacing an entrenched electoral system raises questions of constitutional legitimacy, elite resistance, and institutional continuity in crises.

Bottom line

The intellectual force of sortition lies in a single reframing: elections were never designed to produce a government that resembles the governed, and they measurably don't. If you believe the deepest problems of contemporary democracy are elite capture, money, short-termism, polarization, and the adverse selection of political personalities, then a mechanism that structurally cannot be campaigned for, bought, or gerrymandered is an unusually direct remedy. If you believe accountability and the ability to choose a direction are democracy's essential features, sortition looks like a cure that removes an organ. The most defensible position, held by many deliberative democrats, is that sortition and election are complementary—that a well-designed system uses each where its distinctive virtues apply.

In Defense of Elections: An Impassioned Op-Ed by a Man Who Has Not Approved of a Single Elected Official Since 1994

Guest column by Gerald Fenwick, concerned citizen, former board member of the Hillcrest Homeowners Association (resigned in protest)

Lately I've been hearing a lot of chatter about something called "sortition" — the barbaric proposal that we fill legislatures by random selection from the general population, like a jury, or a bingo hall, or the Athenian democracy that invented the concept we are currently pretending to practice.

As a lifelong defender of the electoral system, I must speak out. Because there is one thing I know for certain: the American people cannot be trusted.

Now, I want to be precise here, because my critics will try to twist my words. I am not saying the American people can't be trusted to choose the government. Obviously they can be trusted to do that. That's sacred. That's the whole thing. I'm saying they can't be trusted to be in the government. Choosing is fine. Serving is unthinkable.

Think about it. If we picked legislators at random, we could end up with some guy who doesn't understand fiscal policy, thinks NATO is a brand of mattress, and gets all his information from a podcast. Whereas under our current system, the voters — the very same people, statistically identical, drawn from the very same pool — carefully select which of those guys gets to do it. That is the difference between chaos and civilization.

The Competence Question

Sortition advocates like to point out that randomly selected citizens would include teachers, nurses, plumbers, farmers, small business owners, and the occasional accountant. To which I say: exactly. My legislature is not a Home Depot.

I want experts. I want people who have devoted their entire lives to the study of governance. And when I look at the résumés of my current representatives, I see exactly that: a man who inherited a car dealership, a woman who was briefly on a reality dating program, a retired dentist, three separate guys named Chad who each raised eleven million dollars from strangers, and my congressman, who, and I want to be fair to him here, was a fantastic high school football coach.

These are not random people. These are people who wanted it. And nothing in human history has ever gone wrong because power was handed to the people who wanted it most.

The Accountability Argument

Here's the crux of it. Under elections, if a politician betrays you, you can vote them out. This is the beating heart of democracy, and it is why I have voted my representative out in every single election since 1994 — a streak interrupted only by the fact that he has won all of them, by twenty-two points, in a district that was drawn by his former chief of staff using a computer program and, I suspect, a Ouija board.

The point is, he is accountable. He knows that if he ever truly crosses the line, roughly 94% of incumbents will be reelected, and he could easily be among the other 6%. That keeps a man honest. You can see the fear in his eyes at the ribbon-cuttings.

Under sortition, by contrast, a citizen legislator would serve one term and then go home forever, with no reelection to raise money for, no donors to please, no party leadership to obey, and no incentive whatsoever except to do a decent job and go back to their actual life. Chilling. Who would they be answerable to? Their own conscience? Have you met a conscience? They don't return your calls either.

On the Matter of Lotteries and Dignity

Several of my neighbors have raised what I consider the most powerful objection: it's undignified to choose leaders by lottery.

And they're right. Leadership should be earned — through a rigorous, meritocratic process in which candidates spend eighteen months begging billionaires for money, filming themselves eating regional foods, and workshopping a story about their grandfather until it makes a focus group in Ohio cry.

Only through this crucible do we discover a person's true character: specifically, their willingness to do all of that. Which, I'll admit, is not a trait I would want in a babysitter, a surgeon, a business partner, or a houseguest. But in the people who control the military, it's essential.

They Say "Juries." I Say: Juries!

The sortition crowd's favorite trick is to bring up juries. "We trust twelve randomly selected citizens to decide whether a man spends the rest of his life in prison," they smirk, "but not to set the tax code?"

Yes. Correct. Next question.

Look, a jury decides one case, with expert testimony, structured deliberation, rules of evidence, and a duty to reach a considered judgment. A legislature does something completely different: it decides one thousand cases, with expert testimony, structured deliberation, rules of procedure, and — no, hold on. Let me start over.

A Concession, Which I Immediately Withdraw

I'll grant the sortition people one small thing. When Ireland put a randomly selected citizens' assembly on the abortion question, and when British Columbia put ordinary people in charge of electoral reform, and when various cities have run citizen assemblies on climate policy, the participants generally showed up, read the briefings, listened to opposing experts, took it deadly seriously, changed their minds when presented with evidence, and produced recommendations that a strong majority of the public supported.

But here's what those studies conveniently omit: it's weird. It made everyone uncomfortable. There was no yelling. No one raised money. Nobody's brother-in-law got a contract. It felt, frankly, un-American, and also un-Irish, and I say that as someone with an Irish grandmother whose story I have workshopped extensively.

In Conclusion

Friends, the choice before us is stark.

On one hand: a system where power is distributed randomly across the whole citizenry, where nobody campaigns, nobody owes a donor, nobody gerrymanders, and the legislature actually looks like the country.

On the other: the system we have now, which I have described as "broken," "captured," "a circus," and "honestly the worst it's ever been" in every conversation I have had at every barbecue for thirty-one years.

I know which one I'm sticking with. Because there's an old saying, and I think about it often: better the devil you know.

And I want to be clear about something. I do not know that devil. I have never met him. He has never held a town hall. His office responds to my letters with a form email that misspells my name.

But he was elected. And that, my friends, is what makes us free.

Gerald Fenwick's forthcoming book, Everyone in Charge Is an Idiot and Also Please Don't Change Anything*, is available for preorder.*

The Lottery of Liberty

A speech in favor of government by sortition

Friends, neighbors, fellow citizens —

Let me begin with a question so simple that we have trained ourselves not to ask it:

Why do we let people who want power be the ones who get power?

Think about that. In almost every other domain of life, we regard the hunger for authority as a warning sign. We do not hand the church collection plate to the man who campaigns hardest to hold it. We do not give the loaded weapon to the person most eager to fire it. Yet in the one arena where the stakes are highest — where we decide who goes to war, who goes to prison, who goes hungry, who goes bankrupt from a hospital bill — we have built an entire system designed to select for ambition, for showmanship, for the willingness to spend two years begging billionaires for money.

And then we act surprised when the results are what they are.

What we actually have

Let us be honest about the machine we call representative democracy in America today.

To run for the United States Senate, you need millions of dollars. Not to persuade voters — to rent their attention thirty seconds at a time. Which means that long before a single citizen casts a single ballot, a prior election has already been held. It is conducted quietly, in ballrooms and on conference calls, and the electorate consists of a few thousand donors. By the time the choice reaches you, the menu has already been written.

We call this "choosing our leaders." I call it ratifying someone else's shortlist.

And who ends up in that chamber? A body far wealthier than the country it governs. Overwhelmingly lawyers, executives, and professional politicians. People who, on the day they are sworn in, are handed a phone and a call sheet and told: your real job is to raise money for the next campaign, starting now. Studies of decades of federal policy have found that the preferences of ordinary citizens have a near-zero independent effect on what actually becomes law, while the preferences of economic elites and organized interests predict outcomes with grim reliability.

Meanwhile, Congress polls somewhere near the popularity of head lice — and better than ninety percent of its members win reelection anyway. Districts are drawn so that representatives choose their voters instead of the reverse. Primaries reward the loudest and the angriest. Every vote a legislator casts is shadowed by the question: how will this play in the next cycle, and will my donors stay with me?

This is not a system that has been corrupted. This is a system that is functioning exactly as its incentives dictate. You cannot fix it by electing better people, because the election is the filter, and the filter is broken. You can pour clean water into a rusted pipe all day long. It will come out rust.

The idea we abandoned

Here is what history knows and we have forgotten.

For nearly two centuries, the Athenians — the people who invented the word democracy — filled almost all of their public offices by lot. Their council of five hundred, their juries of hundreds, their magistrates: chosen at random from citizens who put their names forward. They had a machine for it, the kleroterion, a slab of stone with slots and bronze tokens and a randomizing tube. They built a piece of civic technology whose entire purpose was to make it impossible to buy an office.

Athenians regarded elections as an aristocratic device — a mechanism for selecting the notable, the wealthy, the well-spoken. Aristotle said so plainly: the lot is democratic, election is oligarchic. Venice used elaborate lotteries to choose its Doge for five hundred years, precisely to break the grip of rival dynasties. Florence drew officials from leather bags.

They were not naive. They were cynical — in the best way. They understood that concentrated power attracts the ambitious like blood attracts sharks, and the only reliable defense is to make the prize unwinnable.

What I am proposing

So here is the proposal, plainly stated.

Replace election with sortition. Fill our legislatures — and ultimately our executive offices — with ordinary citizens chosen by random lottery from the population, stratified so that the body mirrors the nation in age, region, race, gender, income, and education. Not a sample of the ambitious. A sample of America.

Make it work like this:

  • Service is a civic duty, like jury duty, but honored and compensated — a full professional salary, job protection, childcare, housing, relocation support, so that a warehouse worker in Toledo and a nurse in Tucson can serve as easily as a corporate lawyer in Manhattan.
  • Terms are fixed, staggered, and non-renewable. You serve. You go home. You return to live under the laws you wrote. There is no next campaign, because there is no campaign at all.
  • Members receive real training and real staff — nonpartisan analysts, subject-matter experts on call, structured deliberation, adversarial briefings from all sides so that no single expert becomes a puppeteer.
  • Lobbyists lose their leverage entirely. What do you offer a legislator who cannot be reelected, cannot be primaried, and returns to private life in two years? Campaign contributions become meaningless when there are no campaigns. Bribery becomes a felony with no plausible deniability.

"But ordinary people aren't qualified"

Now — I can hear it. I have heard it every time I have made this argument.

The average person isn't equipped to govern.

My friends, we already trust the average person with the most awesome power the state possesses: we let twelve strangers, chosen at random, decide whether a fellow human being spends the rest of his life in a cage. We do this thousands of times a day. And juries, given evidence, given time, given the seriousness of the task, are remarkably good at it. They deliberate. They surprise us. They rise.

And this is not theory. Ireland put a randomly selected citizens' assembly on the most explosive questions in its national life — marriage equality, abortion — questions that had paralyzed its politicians for a generation. Ordinary Irish people sat down for months, heard testimony, argued, and produced recommendations that went to referendum and passed. British Columbia's citizens' assembly on electoral reform produced a proposal that professional political scientists praised as sophisticated. France convened a citizens' convention on climate that generated more ambitious policy in nine months than its parliament had in nine years. Oregon has used citizen review panels to evaluate ballot measures. Mongolia has written deliberative polling into its constitutional process.

Everywhere it has been tried, the same thing happens: normal people, given real information, real time, and real responsibility, deliberate better than the professionals. Better — because they have no donors to please, no party whip in the hallway, no reelection to survive, no cable-news hit to book. They have only the problem in front of them and each other.

The question was never whether ordinary citizens are capable. The question is whether the people currently in power find that possibility convenient.

What we would gain

Imagine a legislature where roughly half the members are women — because half the country is. Where working people are present in proportion to their actual numbers. Where the person debating the minimum wage has earned the minimum wage. Where the person debating veterans' health care has waited in that line. Where the person debating student debt is still paying it.

Imagine a chamber that cannot be gerrymandered, because it has no districts to carve. That cannot be captured by primary electorates, because it holds no primaries. That cannot be purchased, because its seats are not for sale at any price.

Imagine a politics in which "electability" is not a word — in which no one has to be photogenic, or rich, or well-connected, or shameless, to serve their country.

And imagine what it would do to us. Right now, citizenship in America means choosing, once every two years, between options someone else selected. Under sortition, every one of us would live with the knowledge that the call might come. That we might be summoned. That the republic might genuinely, personally, ask something of us. That is not a burden. That is the restoration of citizenship itself.

The closing case

I know how radical this sounds. Every expansion of democracy has sounded radical the day before it happened. Universal suffrage was radical. Ending property requirements was radical. The direct election of senators was radical. In each case the guardians of the old arrangement insisted that the people were not ready, were not informed, were not fit.

They were wrong every single time.

We are told to revere the ballot as the sacred heart of freedom. But the ballot, as it exists today, is a permission slip. It permits us to approve one of two people we did not choose, funded by donors we cannot see, to make decisions we will not be consulted on. That is not self-government. That is consent management.

Sortition is not a retreat from democracy. It is democracy without the middleman. It says: this country belongs to all of us equally, and therefore the burden and the honor of governing it should fall on all of us equally, by the impartial hand of chance rather than the partial hand of money.

The Athenians carved their lottery machine out of stone because they understood something we have let ourselves forget: the surest way to keep power from being bought is to make it impossible to seek.

Let us build our own kleroterion.

Not a nation ruled by those who clawed their way to the top — but a nation governed, in rotation, by its own people. By the teacher and the trucker, the farmer and the pharmacist, the veteran and the student, the retired and the young.

Ruling and being ruled in turn.

That was the promise at the very beginning. Let us finally keep it.

Thank you.

Here is a detailed persuasive essay arguing in favor of replacing all elections in the United States with a system of sortition.

The Lottery of Liberty: Why Sortition Must Replace the Scourge of Elections

For over two centuries, the American experiment has been tethered to the sacred cow of elections. We are taught that the right to vote is the bedrock of democracy, the "thunderous voice of the people." But that voice has become a whisper, drowned out by the roar of Super PACs, the hiss of partisan attack ads, and the soft, corrupting clink of campaign contributions. The system is not merely broken; it is a machine designed to fail the very public it claims to serve. The radical, necessary, and profoundly hopeful solution is to scrap elections entirely and replace them with the ancient, tried-and-true method of sortition: the random selection of citizens to hold legislative and executive office.

It is time to face a difficult truth: elections are a proven technology of corruption and division. By replacing them with a system of citizen juries and councils chosen by lottery, we can excise political corruption, surgically remove partisanship, and finally empower ordinary Americans to govern their own country.

The Alchemy of Influence: How Sortition Ends Political Corruption

The primary engine of corruption in the United States is the electoral funding system. A candidate cannot win a national or even a state-level race without raising millions, often hundreds of millions, of dollars. This creates an inherent, inescapable conflict of interest. Politicians are not accountable to the people who voted for them; they are accountable to the donors who financed the campaign that got them elected. This is not a conspiracy theory; it is the cold, mechanical reality of the machine.

Every decision a politician makes is filtered through a lens of donor appeasement. The tax loophole, the watered-down regulation, the military contract for a district back home—these are the transactional currency of the system. Sortition breaks this chain irrevocably. A citizen selected by lottery to serve a single, non-renewable term in a legislative body has no political career to protect. They have no massive war chest to raise. They have no financial backers to repay.

Imagine a Congress composed of 435 randomly selected Americans—a teacher from Ohio, a nurse from Texas, a farmer from Iowa, a small business owner from Maine. The lobbyist’s bribe, the offer of a lucrative board seat after retirement, the implicit threat of a primary challenge from a better-funded opponent—all of these become meaningless. The selected citizen serves for a fixed term (perhaps two or three years) and then returns to their life. The entire multi-billion-dollar industry of political fundraising and influence-peddling collapses overnight. The "revolving door" between government and the private sector slams shut. Sortition doesn't just reduce corruption; it makes the very concept of political bribery strategically worthless.

The Bitter Fracture: Dismantling Partisanship Through Random Representation

The second plague of the current system is hyper-partisanship. Elections are zero-sum games. Every campaign is designed to demonize the opposition, to energize a base through fear and outrage. This manufactured conflict trickles down from the campaign trail into the halls of power, where winning a political fight for the sake of tribal loyalty has become more important than solving problems. A representative is punished for compromise, vilified for bipartisanship.

Sortition offers a cure by changing the very nature of the "representative." An elected official is a professional partisan, chosen by a primary electorate that is far more ideological than the general public. A sortition-selected citizen is a statistical mirror of the nation. The body would be composed of 33% Democrats, 33% Republicans, and 33% Independents and others—provided that is the actual composition of the country.

This is not a recipe for gridlock; it is a recipe for authentic deliberation. Randomly selected citizens, free from the pressure of re-election and the whip of a party leader, are free to listen, learn, and deliberate. They are far more likely to seek consensus and practical solutions because they have no ideological brand to protect. They are not professional debaters; they are human beings facing real-world problems. The incentive to posture and filibuster disappears. In their place emerges a powerful incentive to find the common ground that a selection of ordinary Americans can agree upon.

This system has been tested in "citizens' assemblies" across the globe—in Ireland, Canada, and France—where randomly selected panels tackled deeply divisive issues like abortion, same-sex marriage, and climate change. The results were consistently surprising: these mini-publics, when given time, resources, and respect, produced thoughtful, nuanced recommendations that often broke the partisan logjam that professional politicians could not. Sortition would scale this proven model of deliberative democracy to the national stage.

The Return of the Athenian Promise: Empowering Ordinary People

The final, and most profound, argument for sortition is its power to restore genuine agency and dignity to the average citizen. Under the current system, our political role is passive. We are spectators—consumers of political products every two to four years. We choose between two pre-selected, focus-group-tested candidates, and we have virtually no say in the policies they enact. Our "empowerment" is a shallow, ritualized exercise.

Sortition fundamentally inverts this relationship. It transforms every citizen from a passive voter into a potential ruler. The idea that a person could be called upon to serve their country not by voting but by actually governing is deeply empowering. It says that wisdom, common sense, and a stake in the community are not the exclusive property of a professional political class.

It directly attacks the insidious "elite capture" of our political system. Today, the path to office is paved by connections, money, and media savviness—skills that have nothing to do with good governance. Sortition ensures that the leadership of the country is drawn from the full tapestry of American life. The voice of the single mother working two jobs, the voice of the veteran struggling with PTSD, the voice of the rural farmer and the urban shopkeeper—these voices, which are systematically excluded from our current oligarchic system, would finally have a guaranteed seat at the table. The government would no longer be a distant, alien institution; it would be our neighbors, us.

The objection that ordinary people are unqualified to govern is the final, desperate argument of the elite. It is a self-serving myth. The people who run our government now are not uniquely gifted. They are simply uniquely ambitious. A randomly selected citizen, armed with a staff of non-partisan experts (like the Congressional Budget Office), weeks of intensive study, and a clear mandate to find the best solution, is fully capable of making informed decisions. In many ways, they are better qualified because they bring a crucial element the professionals lack: the lived experience of being subject to the laws they are writing.

Conclusion: A Call to a New Republic

The American Republic was founded on a radical bet: that a citizenry could govern itself. But the founders themselves were wary of the corrupting power of elections and factions. We have seen their worst fears realized. Our electoral system has become a casino for lobbyists, a coliseum for partisan gladiators, and a gilded cage for the common good.

Sortition is not a retreat from democracy. It is a return to its deepest, purest principles. It is a system that cleanses our politics of the poison of money, removes the tribal armor of partisan warfare, and places the ultimate power of decision-making back into the hands of the people from whom it was stolen. The path forward is clear: we must replace the broken machinery of elections with the lottery of liberty. Let us not choose our rulers. Let us become them.

This is a fascinating and increasingly relevant topic in political theory. The idea of replacing or supplementing elections with sortition (random selection) draws on ancient Athenian democracy (where juries and councils were chosen by lot) and modern deliberative democracy experiments (like citizens' juries and assemblies).

Here is an explanation of the supposed benefits and reasons for adopting a nationwide system of sortition, focusing on the three areas you requested.

1. Improving Government Fairness

The core argument for sortition's fairness is that it eliminates the structural biases inherent in the election process itself.

  • Equal Opportunity to Govern: In an election, only a tiny, self-selected fraction of the population can realistically become a legislator. You need ambition, money, connections, a thick skin for public scrutiny, and often a specific career path (law, business, activism). Sortition resets this. It proposes that every citizen has an equal chance of serving, regardless of their background, profession, or ambition. This isn't just about outcome (who is chosen) but about the fundamental opportunity to participate at the highest level.
  • Removes the Tyranny of the Minority of Voters: Elections are often decided by a small, highly engaged, and often partisan slice of the electorate (e.g., primary voters or swing voters in a few key states). This gives that minority enormous power to shape the policy choices of the entire nation. A sortition-based body, selected to be a representative microcosm of the whole population, would be less beholden to the whims of a vocal, unrepresentative few.
  • Neutralizes the "Electioneering" Distortion: The entire election cycle forces candidates to prioritize fundraising, polling, attack ads, and soundbites over thoughtful deliberation and nuanced policy. This creates a system where the best politicians are often those best at campaigning, not those best at governing. Sortition removes the campaign entirely, allowing citizens to focus directly on the substance of policy from day one.

2. Reducing Elite Influence

This is perhaps the most powerful argument from a practical standpoint. Sortition is seen as a direct, structural antidote to the power of money and organized interests.

  • Breaks the Link Between Wealth and Power: In an electoral system, candidates are heavily dependent on fundraising from wealthy donors and corporations. This creates an implicit (and often explicit) obligation to serve those interests. Sortition completely severs this link. A randomly selected citizen has no need to fundraise, no donors to appease, and no personal debt to political action committees (PACs). Their only "campaign" is the civic duty to deliberate in the public interest.
  • Dismantles the "Political Class": Elections create a professional political class with its own incentives, culture, and networks (think lobbying firms, think tanks, party leadership). This class becomes a self-perpetuating elite, often out of touch with the daily lives of ordinary citizens. Sortition introduces a rotating, non-professional citizen body. Members are not career politicians; they are plumbers, teachers, nurses, and retirees who serve a fixed term and then return to their normal lives. This prevents the accumulation of institutional power in a small group.
  • Dilutes the Power of Lobbyists and Special Interests: Lobbyists thrive on predictable, long-term relationships with a small number of powerful repeat players. If legislators are changing every few years and are randomly selected from the public, it becomes far more difficult and expensive for lobbyists to build the trusted relationships needed to influence policy. The legislature becomes a much harder target to capture. The influence of money is drastically reduced because the "cost" of buying influence is no longer a few million dollars in campaign donations but the need to influence the entire diverse, rotating population.

3. Enhancing Democratic Representation

This is where sortition offers its most profound challenge to the current definition of "representation." It focuses on descriptive representation (the body looks like the country) over electoral representation (the body was chosen by a vote).

  • Creates a True Microcosm: Elections consistently produce legislatures that are not demographically representative. They tend to over-represent the wealthy, the well-educated, lawyers, and various dominant ethnic or gender groups. A large enough random sample (e.g., 500-1000 people), by the law of averages, will produce a body whose demographic composition (age, gender, race, income, education, geography) closely mirrors the nation as a whole. This is impossible through elections. A sortition chamber would literally look like the country.
  • Brings Lived Experience into the Room: An elected politician can only ever try to understand the struggles of a single mother, a coal miner, or a young person drowning in student debt. A sortition chamber directly includes those people. Their personal, lived experience becomes a form of expertise that is often more valuable than policy briefs or polling data. This leads to more grounded, empathetic, and practical policy-making that is less reliant on abstract ideology.
  • Changes the Nature of Deliberation: In an elected body, the goal is often to win the next argument or score a partisan point. In a sortition body, where members have no party affiliation, no future re-election to worry about, and a finite term, the incentive is different. The goal becomes to listen, learn, deliberate, and find common ground. This can lead to more thoughtful, consensus-driven outcomes that are less prone to the performative gridlock and hyper-partisanship of traditional legislatures. Proponents argue this leads to decisions perceived as more legitimate because they were made by "ordinary people like us" after careful study.

In Summary: The Core Trade-Off

The primary reason to consider sortition is to shift the focus of democracy from popularity and fundraising (the skills needed to win an election) to deliberation and wisdom (the skills needed to make good policy).

Traditional Elections do well at:

  • Providing accountability (voters can "throw the bums out").
  • Giving a clear mechanism for choosing leaders.
  • Legitimizing decisions through popular mandate.

Sortition does well at:

  • Reducing corruption and elite capture.
  • Producing a body that looks and thinks like the nation.
  • Fostering deliberation and compromise over partisan bickering.

Most modern advocates of sortition do not call for abolishing elections entirely. Instead, they propose a bicameral or hybrid system—for example, an elected house that handles broad direction and accountability, and a sortition-based "Citizens' Assembly" that deliberates on specific complex issues, such as electoral reform, healthcare funding, or climate policy, where broad, fair, and informed judgment is more valuable than political loyalty. The supposed benefit is a democracy that is less easily corrupted and more truly representative of its entire people.

Model Response:

Replace Elections with Sortition: A Democratic Case for Randomly Chosen Leaders

The United States has spent more than two centuries treating elections as synonymous with democracy. We assume that citizens must choose politicians through campaigns, fundraising, advertising, debates, and party competition. Yet the familiar electoral system has produced a government increasingly shaped by wealthy donors, professional political organizations, partisan incentives, and career politicians. Elections are presented as the mechanism that gives ordinary people power, but in practice they often narrow public choice to candidates who can raise immense sums of money, survive a hostile media environment, and appeal to party gatekeepers.

There is a better way. The United States should replace elections with sortition: the selection of legislative and executive leaders through a carefully designed, random process that draws representative citizens from the population. A government chosen by lot would not eliminate every difficulty of governing, but it would directly address some of the deepest failures of the current system. Sortition would weaken the influence of money, reduce partisan polarization, broaden representation, and give ordinary people a meaningful role in public decision-making.

Random selection may initially seem undemocratic. How can people who have not campaigned for office govern responsibly? The answer is that democracy is not fundamentally about selecting the most ambitious political competitors. It is about ensuring that the public—not a wealthy minority, not party organizations, and not a professional political class—holds ultimate authority. Sortition would make government more genuinely representative by giving citizens the same chance to serve that they currently have to vote.

Elections Turn Public Office into a Competition for Money and Power

The central weakness of American elections is not merely that campaigns are expensive. It is that money determines who can realistically compete, what issues receive attention, and which interests gain access to decision-makers. Candidates must raise funds for staff, travel, advertising, consultants, polling, legal compliance, and increasingly sophisticated digital operations. Even candidates who oppose wealthy interests must spend enormous amounts of time soliciting donations from them.

This creates a structural conflict. A politician may sincerely want to represent the public, but remaining competitive requires cultivating donors, political action committees, party leaders, and organized interest groups. Campaign finance laws can limit some abuses, but they do not eliminate the underlying incentive. As long as office is won through expensive competition, candidates will be pressured to serve those who finance and promote that competition.

Sortition would remove the campaign-finance problem at its source. Randomly selected citizens would not need to purchase advertising, build a donor network, hire consultants, or appeal to wealthy patrons. No candidate could promise favorable legislation in exchange for contributions because there would be no campaign to finance. Lobbyists could still present arguments, but they would no longer be able to shape a politician’s electoral future through donations, endorsements, or negative advertising.

This would not magically eliminate corruption. Officials could still accept bribes, misuse authority, or favor friends. But sortition would remove one of the largest and most persistent channels through which private interests influence public policy. Strong ethics rules, financial disclosure, independent oversight, criminal enforcement, and transparent deliberation would address remaining risks. The result would be a system in which corruption is more difficult to organize and easier to detect.

Sortition Would Reduce Partisanship by Ending the Permanent Campaign

America’s political parties are not merely organizations that help citizens choose among candidates. They have become governing institutions that reward loyalty, punish compromise, and treat political opponents as enemies. Elected officials must constantly consider how every vote will affect their reelection prospects, their party standing, their fundraising, and their chances of receiving influential committee assignments.

This permanent campaign encourages short-term thinking. Officials are pushed to favor policies that produce immediate political benefits over those that require patience, compromise, or sacrifice. They are also rewarded for public conflict. A dramatic denunciation of the opposing party may generate media attention and energize a political base, even when private negotiation would produce a better result.

Sortition would change these incentives. Randomly chosen citizens would not owe their position to a party, donor network, or ideological primary electorate. They would not need to perform loyalty for partisan activists or prepare for the next campaign. Because their authority would come from the public selection process rather than electoral victory, they could evaluate proposals on their merits and compromise without fearing political retaliation.

A randomly assembled body would also be less ideologically uniform than a legislature composed largely of professional politicians. It would include people with different occupations, regions, educational backgrounds, ages, racial identities, economic circumstances, and life experiences. Such a group would not be free of disagreement, but its disagreements would be less likely to follow rigid party lines. Citizens might still form coalitions, but those coalitions would have to be built around actual questions of policy rather than inherited partisan identities.

The executive branch could benefit from the same principle. Instead of choosing a president through a polarized national contest, the public could randomly select a representative executive council or a chief executive from a citizen pool, supported by professional administrators and accountable to a randomly selected legislature. This would reduce the personality-centered nature of presidential politics and make governing less dependent on charisma, celebrity, and media performance.

Sortition Would Empower Ordinary People Rather Than Political Specialists

Elections favor people who are unusually willing and able to pursue office. Candidates typically possess strong political ambition, extensive networks, financial resources, public-speaking skills, or connections to political organizations. These qualities may help someone win an election, but they are not the same as wisdom, empathy, integrity, or sound judgment.

A government composed almost entirely of people who want political power is not necessarily representative of the population. Most citizens do not want to spend years campaigning, raising money, attending political events, and exposing their private lives to public scrutiny. Under elections, this reluctance effectively excludes them from office. Sortition would correct that imbalance by making public service a civic responsibility that could reach people who would never volunteer as candidates.

A randomly selected citizen would not need to be an expert on every issue. Neither are elected officials. The difference is that sortition could provide citizens with the resources necessary to govern responsibly: nonpartisan briefings, expert testimony, public hearings, legal counsel, policy analysts, and sufficient time to deliberate. A citizen assembly operating under these conditions could make decisions after hearing competing arguments rather than relying on slogans, party platforms, or campaign advertisements.

Ordinary people routinely make serious decisions in workplaces, communities, families, professional associations, and local institutions. They are capable of learning complicated subjects when given time, information, and a meaningful responsibility. The assumption that only professional politicians can govern is not a fact; it is a habit reinforced by the current system.

Sortition would also make citizenship more substantive. In an electoral democracy, most people participate only intermittently, usually by choosing between a small number of candidates. Under sortition, citizens could serve directly in government, observe policy formation, question experts, and deliberate with people unlike themselves. Even those not selected would know that public office is not reserved for an elite class. Government would become something citizens do, not merely something they watch.

Random Selection Can Be More Representative Than Elections

Elections are often described as a mechanism of representation, but they systematically filter the population. Officeholders are disproportionately wealthy, highly educated, older, male, and professionally connected. People with demanding jobs, caregiving responsibilities, disabilities, limited income, or little interest in political self-promotion are less likely to become candidates.

Random selection can produce a body that more closely resembles the population as a whole. Properly designed sortition would use stratified sampling to ensure demographic and geographic representativeness. It could include citizens from every state, income group, age category, racial community, occupational sector, and educational background. Compensation and support for childcare, transportation, accessibility, and lost wages would allow people of modest means to serve without suffering financial hardship.

Representation matters not only symbolically but substantively. A legislature filled with teachers, nurses, mechanics, small-business owners, caregivers, farmers, technicians, students, retirees, and service workers would approach public problems differently from one dominated by lawyers, wealthy professionals, and career politicians. People who have experienced medical debt, insecure housing, disability barriers, underfunded schools, or precarious employment would bring forms of knowledge that are often absent from elected institutions.

Elections can reward candidates who are skilled at presenting themselves as representative. Sortition would make representation a structural feature of government. Instead of asking whether a politician speaks for ordinary people, the system would place ordinary people in the room where decisions are made.

Sortition Would Encourage Deliberation Rather Than Performance

Modern politics is heavily shaped by the demands of public performance. Candidates must produce memorable messages, respond instantly to controversies, simplify complicated proposals, and appeal to segmented audiences. This environment rewards confidence and emotional impact, not necessarily careful reasoning.

A randomly selected governing body could be designed around deliberation. Citizens would receive balanced information, hear advocates from multiple perspectives, ask questions, and discuss consequences before voting. They could work in small groups, consult independent experts, and revise their views as they learned more. Decisions would be based less on which side had the most effective advertisement and more on which arguments survived sustained examination.

Deliberative institutions can also reduce misinformation. A citizen who hears evidence directly, questions its source, and compares it with competing claims is better positioned to judge credibility than someone exposed to thousands of targeted campaign messages. The goal would not be to create citizens who agree on everything. It would be to create decision-makers who can disagree intelligently and reach conclusions without treating disagreement as treason.

A Responsible System Would Combine Sortition with Expertise and Accountability

Critics often argue that randomly chosen citizens would lack the technical knowledge required to manage a modern government. This objection deserves serious attention, but it does not justify preserving elections. The solution is not to abandon democratic control; it is to distinguish between making public decisions and performing professional administration.

Randomly selected citizens could establish priorities, approve laws, oversee budgets, and hold officials accountable. Career civil servants, scientists, engineers, diplomats, economists, and other specialists could provide expertise and carry out lawful decisions. Experts would advise rather than rule. Their knowledge would be essential, but ultimate authority would remain with representatives drawn from the public.

This arrangement would resemble a jury system. Jurors are not expected to know every detail of criminal law or forensic science before serving. They hear evidence, receive instructions, deliberate, and decide. The legitimacy of their role comes not from prior specialization but from impartial participation under a defined process.

Sortition would also require robust safeguards. Terms should be limited. Officials should face strict conflict-of-interest rules, public disclosure requirements, independent ethics enforcement, and transparent proceedings. Citizens should be protected from intimidation and given secure channels for reporting misconduct. Decisions should be reviewable under constitutional standards, and courts should remain independent. A system of random selection must be designed carefully, but so must every democratic system.

The Objection of Incompetence Applies to Elections as Well

Some critics fear that random citizens could be ignorant, irresponsible, or vulnerable to manipulation. Yet elections do not guarantee competence. They select people who are effective at winning campaigns, not necessarily people who understand policy, resist corruption, or govern wisely. Voters often choose among candidates based on party identity, name recognition, emotional appeal, or incomplete information. The electoral system has no reliable test for expertise or integrity.

Moreover, elected officials are not immune to manipulation. They can be influenced by donors, lobbyists, party strategists, media consultants, ideological organizations, and electoral polling. In some respects, randomly selected citizens may be less vulnerable because they do not depend on these networks for continued access to power.

The proper comparison is not between sortition and an imaginary perfect electorate. It is between sortition and the actual electoral system, with all its corruption, misinformation, polarization, and unequal influence. A citizen who begins with limited knowledge but receives balanced instruction and deliberates openly may be better prepared to decide than a professional politician whose incentives are distorted by fundraising and reelection.

Sortition Would Restore the Meaning of Political Equality

The deepest argument for sortition is moral. Democracy rests on the principle that citizens are political equals. But elections often treat citizens unequally. Wealthy people can make larger contributions, gain greater access, and support candidates or causes capable of dominating public attention. Party insiders have more influence over nominations. Professional political networks are better positioned to shape policy. Ordinary citizens may have the formal right to vote, but their practical influence is often much weaker.

Sortition would give every citizen a comparable chance to serve. It would not make everyone equally wealthy or equally influential in every public debate, but it would prevent public office from becoming a competition reserved for the ambitious and well-connected. Political equality would become more than the right to mark a ballot every few years. It would mean that any citizen could be called upon to help govern.

That possibility would also encourage humility among officials. A randomly selected representative would know that authority is temporary and conditional. The person sitting across the table might be a warehouse worker, a parent, a recent immigrant, a veteran, or a neighbor from a different political tradition. Governing would become less about belonging to a superior class and more about fulfilling a shared civic duty.

Replacing Elections Is Bold, but the Current System Is Already Failing

No democratic arrangement is risk-free. Sortition could produce poor decisions, internal conflict, or manipulation if badly designed. It would require constitutional changes, public education, administrative support, and continuous evaluation. But the existence of risks is not an argument for preserving a system whose failures are increasingly visible.

The United States faces political corruption, deep partisanship, declining trust, unequal representation, and a widening gap between citizens and institutions. Elections have not solved these problems because many of them are built into the electoral process itself. A system that requires enormous sums of money, rewards permanent campaigning, and selects a narrow professional class cannot be expected to consistently represent the public as a whole.

Sortition offers a fundamentally different democratic principle: public power should be entrusted not to those most eager to acquire it, but to citizens selected from the public and supported in carrying out their responsibility. It would reduce the power of money, weaken party domination, broaden representation, and make government more directly accountable to ordinary people.

The United States should therefore replace elections for legislative and executive leadership with a carefully regulated system of random citizen selection. Democracy should not be a spectator sport in which citizens choose among competing political brands. It should be a shared institution in which ordinary people govern themselves. Sortition would bring that ideal closer to reality by ensuring that public office belongs not to a permanent political class, but to the people themselves.

Sortition is not a novel idea; its roots lie deep in the history of democracy itself. Ancient Athens, often celebrated as the birthplace of democracy, relied heavily on sortition to fill most public offices. Eliminating Political Corruption

One of the most compelling arguments for replacing elections with sortition is its ability to dismantle systemic political corruption. In the current electoral system, candidates are often dependent on campaign contributions from corporations, interest groups, and wealthy donors.
