Democracy by Lottery: Why Sortition Is the Revolution American Governance Needs

An Argument for Replacing Elections with Random Citizen Selection

I. Introduction

The American experiment in self-governance has lasted nearly two and a half centuries, and for much of that time, the act of casting a ballot has been regarded as the sacred foundation of democratic legitimacy. Elections are celebrated as the purest expression of the people's will, the mechanism through which citizens hold power accountable and choose their leaders. Yet beneath this reverence lies an uncomfortable truth: the American electoral system, as it currently operates, is not a mechanism of popular empowerment. It is a sophisticated apparatus for concentrating power among the wealthy, entrenching a professional political class, partisan donors, and corporate interest groups. From the ever-rising cost of campaigns to the duopoly of the Democratic and Republican parties, from gerrymandering to voter suppression, from the revolving door between government and lobbying firms to the pervasive influence of dark money, the evidence is overwhelming that elections in the United States have become a vehicle for oligarchy rather than democracy.

It is time to consider a radical alternative—one that is not radical at all, but rather one of the oldest and most proven methods of democratic governance in human history. Sortition, the selection of political representatives and leaders through random lottery from among the citizenry, offers a path to genuine democratic renewal. Used by the ancient Athenians, the birthplace of democracy itself, and employed in various forms throughout history and in contemporary deliberative processes around the world, sortition has the potential to dismantle the corrupt structures that define modern American politics. By replacing elections with random selection, the United States could eliminate the corrosive influence of money in politics, break the stranglehold of partisan polarization, and return power to the very people democracy is supposed to serve: ordinary citizens.

This essay argues that sortition should replace elections at all levels of American government—local, state, and federal—and that doing so would represent the most significant and beneficial transformation of democratic governance since the founding of the Republic.

II. The Case Against Elections: A System in Crisis

A. The Corrupting Influence of Money

To understand why sortition is necessary, one must first confront the depth of the crisis afflicting the American electoral system. The most glaring and well-documented failure is the role of money in politics. The 2010 Supreme Court decision in Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission opened the floodgates for unlimited corporate and union spending on political campaigns, but the problem predates that ruling by decades. In the 2020 election cycle alone, total spending on federal elections exceeded $14 billion, more than double the amount spent just eight years earlier. The 2024 cycle shattered even those records.

This staggering expenditure is not a sign of democratic health; it is a symptom of democratic decay. When campaigns require tens or hundreds of millions of dollars to compete, candidates are forced to become fundraisers first and public servants second. They spend an estimated 40 to 70 percent of their time in office dialing for dollars, calling wealthy donors and attending fundraising events rather than legislating, meeting with constituents, or studying policy. The result is a government that is responsive not to the median voter but to the median donor—a person who is overwhelmingly wealthy, white, male, and connected to corporate interests.

The consequences are measurable and devastating. Political scientists Martin Gilens and Benjamin Page, in their landmark 2014 study analyzing 1,779 policy issues, concluded that "economic elites and organized groups representing business interests have substantial independent impacts on U.S. government policy, while average citizens and mass-based interest groups have little or no independent influence." This is not a democracy. This is a system in which elections serve as a theatrical performance, giving the appearance of popular choice while the real decisions are made in boardrooms and donor retreats.

Sortition eliminates this problem entirely. When leaders are chosen by lottery, there is nothing to fundraise for. There are no campaign contributions to solicit, no Super PACs to court, no corporate sponsors to appease. A randomly selected citizen arrives in office owing nothing to anyone—not to a party, not to a donor, not to a lobbyist. Their loyalty is to the public interest, because they have no other constituency to serve.

B. The Professional Political Class and the Revolving Door

Elections in the United States have produced a professional political class that is profoundly disconnected from the lives of ordinary Americans. Members of Congress are, on average, significantly wealthier than the constituents they represent. As of recent data, the median net worth of a member of Congress is over $1 million, while the median net worth of an American household is roughly $190,000. More than half of all members of Congress are millionaires. This is not a representative cross-section of the American people; it is an aristocracy that has learned to speak the language of the common citizen while serving the interests of the uncommon one.

Moreover, the revolving door between government and the private sector ensures that even well-intentioned politicians are shaped by the expectation of lucrative post-government careers. Former members of Congress routinely become lobbyists, consultants, and corporate board members, leveraging the relationships and insider knowledge they acquired in public service for private profit. This creates a perverse incentive structure in which public office is treated not as a civic duty but as a stepping stone to personal enrichment.

Sortition shatters this dynamic. A randomly selected citizen—a teacher, a nurse, a factory worker, a small business owner—has no political career to advance, no lobbying firm waiting with a seven-figure salary, no incentive to curry favor with corporate interests. They serve their term and return to their community, their perspective permanently enriched by the experience of governance but their personal finances untouched by the corrupting machinery of professional politics.

C. Partisan Polarization and the Two-Party Duopoly

The American electoral system, with its single-member districts and winner-take-all rules, has produced a rigid two-party duopoly that bears primary responsibility for the paralyzing polarization that now defines American politics. The Democratic and Republican parties do not merely compete; they have become tribal identities, each defining itself primarily in opposition to the other. Primary elections, which are dominated by the most ideologically extreme voters, pull candidates toward the fringes. The result is a Congress in which compromise is punished, bipartisanship is derided as weakness, and governance has become a zero-sum war.

This polarization is not an accident; it is a structural feature of electoral systems. When the path to power runs through party primaries, politicians must appeal to party bases rather than to the broader electorate. They must demonize the opposition, amplify cultural grievances, and resist any policy that could be portrayed as a concession to the other side. The incentive structure of elections rewards division, not unity.

Sortition bypasses parties entirely. A randomly selected legislature would contain no party whips, no party platforms, no party discipline. Members would be free to evaluate each issue on its merits, to form coalitions based on shared values and evidence rather than partisan loyalty, and to seek compromise without fear of being "primaried" by an ideological extremist. Research on citizens' assemblies around the world—from Ireland to British Columbia to France—consistently shows that when ordinary people are given balanced information, time to deliberate, and freedom from partisan pressure, they produce thoughtful, moderate, and broadly acceptable policy recommendations.

D. Voter Suppression, Gerrymandering, and the Illusion of Choice

Even setting aside money and partisanship, the mechanics of American elections are riddled with structural injustices that undermine the principle of equal representation. Gerrymandering—the practice of drawing electoral district boundaries to favor one party—has reached such extremes that in many states, the outcome of legislative elections is effectively predetermined before a single vote is cast. In the 2018 midterm elections, for example, Democratic candidates for the U.S. House received 53% of the statewide vote in Pennsylvania but won only 9 of 18 seats, a disparity directly attributable to gerrymandered maps.

Voter suppression efforts—including strict voter ID laws, purges of voter rolls, reductions in polling places in minority communities, and restrictions on mail-in voting—disproportionately disenfranchise communities of color, low-income citizens, young people, and the elderly. These are not isolated incidents; they are systematic efforts to shape the electorate to produce desired outcomes, a practice that is fundamentally antithetical to democratic principles.

Sortition renders all of these tactics irrelevant. There are no districts to gerrymander when representatives are chosen at large. There are no voters to suppress when participation is not voluntary but mandatory. Every citizen has an equal probability of selection, regardless of race, income, geography, or political affiliation. The result is a body that is, by mathematical necessity, a far more accurate reflection of the American people than any elected legislature has ever been.

III. The Case for Sortition: Ancient Wisdom, Modern Evidence

A. The Athenian Legacy

The argument for sortition is not a novel invention; it is a return to the roots of democracy itself. In ancient Athens, the world's first democracy, the primary method of selecting public officials was not election but lottery. The Athenians understood something that modern political science has largely forgotten: that elections are inherently aristocratic, tending to favor the wealthy, the well-connected, and the rhetorically gifted. As the philosopher Aristotle observed, "The appointment of magistrates by lot is thought to be democratic, and the election of them oligarchic."

The Athenians used sortition to fill hundreds of government positions, including the Boule, a council of 500 citizens chosen annually by lot that set the agenda for the Assembly and oversaw the day-to-day administration of the city-state. They also used it to select jurors for the popular courts, which could number in the hundreds or even thousands for important cases. The system was not perfect—it excluded women, slaves, and non-citizens—but within its framework, it achieved a level of direct citizen participation in governance that no modern electoral democracy has matched.

The Athenian experience demonstrates that sortition is not a utopian fantasy; it is a proven system of governance that sustained the world's first democracy for nearly two centuries. The question is not whether sortition can work, but whether we have the courage to learn from the civilization that invented democracy in the first place.

B. Modern Evidence: Citizens' Assemblies and Deliberative Democracy

In recent decades, a growing body of evidence from around the world has demonstrated the effectiveness of sortition-based deliberative processes. Citizens' assemblies—bodies of randomly selected citizens who are given time, resources, and expert testimony to study complex issues and make recommendations—have been used with remarkable success in countries including Ireland, Canada, France, Australia, and the United Kingdom.

The most celebrated example is the Irish Citizens' Assembly of 2016-2018, which was convened to study several contentious constitutional issues, including abortion, climate change, and fixed-term parliaments. The assembly consisted of 99 randomly selected citizens and a chairperson, chosen to be representative of the Irish population in terms of age, gender, geography, and social class. After months of deliberation, the assembly recommended the legalization of abortion, a recommendation that was subsequently approved by 66.4% of voters in a national referendum. The assembly's work on climate action similarly produced ambitious recommendations that were adopted by the Irish parliament.

The French Convention Citoyenne pour le Climat (Citizens' Convention on Climate), convened in 2019, brought together 150 randomly selected citizens to develop proposals for reducing France's greenhouse gas emissions. The convention produced 149 proposals, many of which were adopted by President Macron and the French legislature. The process was widely praised for its ability to break through the partisan gridlock that had long stymied climate policy.

In British Columbia and Ontario, citizens' assemblies on electoral reform produced thoughtful recommendations that, while not always adopted by voters in subsequent referendums, demonstrated that ordinary citizens are fully capable of grappling with complex institutional questions when given the time and resources to do so.

These examples are not anomalies; they are part of a growing global movement toward deliberative democracy that recognizes the limitations of electoral politics and the untapped potential of ordinary citizens. The consistent finding across all of these processes is the same: when people are selected randomly, given balanced information, and afforded the time and space to deliberate, they produce decisions that are more thoughtful, more representative, and more oriented toward the common good than those produced by elected officials.

C. The Epistemic Argument: Why Random Selection Produces Better Governance

There is a powerful epistemic argument for sortition—that is, an argument about the quality of knowledge and judgment that a randomly selected body can bring to governance. The political philosopher Hélène Landemore, in her influential book Open Government: Reinventing Popular Rule for the Twenty-First Century, argues that cognitive diversity—the variety of perspectives, experiences, and problem-solving approaches that different people bring to a group—is more important for good decision-making than individual expertise.

Elected legislatures, by their nature, tend to be composed of people with similar backgrounds: lawyers, businesspeople, career politicians. This homogeneity of experience produces a homogeneity of thought, which in turn produces blind spots, groupthink, and an inability to anticipate the consequences of policy for communities that are not represented in the room. A randomly selected legislature, by contrast, would include people from every walk of life—people who have experienced poverty, disability, discrimination, and the daily struggles of navigating systems that elected officials only read about in briefing papers.

The mathematician and political theorist Scott Page has formalized this insight in his work on the "diversity trumps ability" theorem, which demonstrates that under the right conditions, a diverse group of problem-solvers will outperform a group of individually more capable but less diverse problem-solvers. Applied to governance, this means that a randomly selected body of ordinary citizens, drawing on the full range of American experience and knowledge, is likely to produce better policy outcomes than a body of elected officials who, however individually talented, share a narrow set of life experiences and professional backgrounds.

D. The Equality Argument: One Person, One Chance

At its deepest level, the argument for sortition is an argument about equality. Elections, for all their democratic rhetoric, are fundamentally unequal. They give more weight to the preferences of those who are more politically engaged, more affluent, more educated, and more connected. They give less weight to the preferences of the poor, the marginalized, the disengaged, and the disenfranchised. The result is a system in which some citizens' voices count more than others—a result that is incompatible with the democratic principle of political equality.

Sortition, by contrast, embodies political equality in its purest form. Every citizen has an exactly equal probability of being selected. There is no advantage to wealth, fame, connections, or political activism. The single mother working two jobs has the same chance of serving in Congress as the corporate CEO. The retired veteran in rural Mississippi has the same chance as the tech entrepreneur in Silicon Valley. This is not merely a theoretical ideal; it is a mathematical reality that no electoral system can replicate.

Moreover, sortition ensures that the resulting body is descriptively representative of the population—that is, it mirrors the demographic composition of the society it serves. An elected legislature can (and often does) fail to reflect the racial, gender, socioeconomic, or age diversity of the population. A randomly selected legislature, if drawn properly, cannot. This descriptive representation matters not only as a matter of justice but as a matter of governance: a body that looks like America is more likely to govern for America.

IV. Addressing the Objections

A. "Ordinary Citizens Are Not Qualified to Govern"

This is the most common objection to sortition, and it is the one that most clearly reveals the elitist assumptions underlying the defense of elections. The claim that ordinary citizens are incapable of governing rests on a profound misunderstanding of both the nature of governance and the capabilities of ordinary people.

First, it is important to note that sortition does not mean the absence of expertise. A randomly selected legislature would have access to the same expert advisors, civil servants, and policy analysts that elected legislatures currently employ. The role of the legislator is not to be a subject-matter expert on every issue but to exercise judgment, weigh competing values, and make decisions in the public interest. These are capacities that every adult citizen possesses, and they are capacities that are, if anything, enhanced by the diversity of experience that a randomly selected body brings to the table.

Second, the claim that ordinary citizens are unqualified to govern is empirically contradicted by the experience of citizens' assemblies around the world. The Irish Citizens' Assembly, the French Convention on Climate, and dozens of other deliberative processes have demonstrated that ordinary people, when given adequate information and time, are fully capable of understanding complex issues and making sound recommendations. Indeed, the evidence suggests that they often do so more effectively than elected officials, precisely because they are free from the distorting pressures of partisanship, fundraising, and re-election.

Third, the "qualifications" argument is hypocritical when applied to elected officials. Many of the most consequential decisions in American history—decisions about war, economic policy, and civil rights—have been made by elected officials who were spectacularly unqualified, whether by virtue of ignorance, ideology, or corruption. The question is not whether randomly selected citizens will be perfect decision-makers; it is whether they will be better decision-makers than the people who currently hold power. The evidence strongly suggests that they will.

B. "Sortition Would Be Vulnerable to Manipulation"

Critics sometimes argue that a sortition system could be manipulated—that the selection process could be rigged, that the pool of eligible citizens could be narrowed, or that the selected body could be unduly influenced by staff, lobbyists, or media. These are legitimate concerns, but they are concerns that can be addressed through careful institutional design.

The selection process can be made transparent and auditable, using publicly verifiable random number generators and independent oversight bodies. The pool of eligible citizens can be defined broadly, with reasonable exemptions for those with severe cognitive impairments or active criminal proceedings, and with mandatory service provisions similar to jury duty. The selected body can be insulated from outside influence through strict conflict-of-interest rules, transparency requirements, and the provision of independent, nonpartisan staff and expert advisors.

Moreover, it is worth noting that elections are far more vulnerable to manipulation than sortition would be. Elections can be manipulated through gerrymandering, voter suppression, misinformation campaigns, foreign interference, and the sheer power of money. Sortition eliminates most of these vulnerabilities by removing the incentive to manipulate outcomes: there is no election to win, no district to gerrymander, no voter to suppress. The only way to manipulate a sortition system is to corrupt the selection process itself, which is far easier to detect and prevent than the myriad ways in which elections are currently corrupted.

C. "People Don't Want to Serve"

Some argue that randomly selected citizens would be unwilling or unable to serve, either because of the demands on their time or because of a lack of interest in politics. This objection underestimates both the civic capacity of ordinary people and the power of institutional design to facilitate participation.

First, service in a sortition-based legislature would be compensated at a level sufficient to replace the citizen's ordinary income, ensuring that participation is not limited to those who can afford to take time off work. Childcare, eldercare, and other support services would be provided. The term of service would be limited—perhaps two to four years—after which the citizen would return to their normal life.

Second, the experience of jury duty demonstrates that ordinary citizens are willing to serve when called upon, even when the burden is significant. Jury duty is widely regarded as one of the most important civic responsibilities in a democracy, and compliance rates are high despite the inconvenience. Sortition for legislative service would be framed in the same terms: as a fundamental civic duty, essential to the functioning of democracy.

Third, the objection that people are not interested in politics is itself a product of the current system. When politics is dominated by professional politicians, partisan warfare, and corporate money, it is no wonder that many citizens feel alienated and disengaged. A system that genuinely empowers ordinary people—that gives them real responsibility, real resources, and real influence over the decisions that shape their lives—is likely to generate far more engagement and enthusiasm than a system in which their only role is to choose between two pre-selected candidates every few years.

D. "Sortition Would Be Unstable or Inefficient"

Critics sometimes argue that a randomly selected legislature would be unstable, lacking the institutional knowledge and continuity that elected officials develop over time. This concern can be addressed through a mixed model in which a portion of the body is selected each year, ensuring overlap between incoming and outgoing members, and in which professional staff and civil servants provide institutional continuity.

In fact, the evidence from citizens' assemblies suggests that sortition-based bodies are remarkably efficient and productive. The Irish Citizens' Assembly completed its work on multiple complex issues in less than two years. The French Convention on Climate produced 149 detailed proposals in seven months. These bodies were able to move quickly and decisively precisely because they were not constrained by partisan calculations, electoral timelines, or the need to posture for the cameras.

V. A Blueprint for Sortition in the United States

Implementing sortition in the United States would require a fundamental restructuring of American governance, but the basic framework is straightforward and can be adapted to existing institutional structures.

A. The Legislature

The U.S. Congress would be replaced by a National Citizens' Assembly of approximately 1,000 members, selected annually by stratified random sampling from the adult citizen population. The assembly would be stratified to ensure proportional representation by race, gender, age, income, geography, and other relevant demographic categories. Members would serve staggered two-year terms, with half the body rotating each year to ensure continuity.

The assembly would operate through a combination of plenary sessions and specialized committees, with each member serving on one or more committees focused on specific policy areas. Committees would have access to independent expert advisors, and all proceedings would be transparent and publicly accessible.

B. The Executive

The President would be selected by lottery from among the members of the National Citizens' Assembly, serving a single four-year term. Alternatively, a collective executive—a council of five to seven randomly selected citizens—could be chosen to serve as a collegial presidency, making decisions by supermajority vote. This would distribute executive power more broadly and reduce the risks associated with concentrating authority in a single individual.

Cabinet positions and agency heads would be selected by lottery from among citizens with relevant professional experience, identified through a supplementary selection process that ensures a baseline of expertise while maintaining the principle of random selection.

C. State and Local Government

State legislatures and local governing bodies would be replaced by state and local citizens' assemblies, selected by the same principles of stratified random sampling. The size of these bodies would be proportional to the population of the jurisdiction, with minimum sizes sufficient to ensure meaningful deliberation and maximum sizes sufficient to ensure manageability.

D. Safeguards and Complementary Institutions

A sortition-based system would be complemented by several important institutional safeguards:

  • A Constitutional Court with the power to review legislation for compliance with fundamental rights and constitutional principles, ensuring that the majority cannot use its power to oppress minorities.
  • A free and independent press to inform the public and hold the assembly accountable.
  • Referendums and initiatives allowing citizens to vote directly on major constitutional questions and to challenge legislation they believe is unjust.
  • Robust transparency requirements, including public proceedings, open records, and mandatory disclosure of all communications between assembly members and outside parties.

VI. The Transformative Potential of Sortition

The adoption of sortition would not merely reform American governance; it would transform it in ways that are difficult to fully anticipate but that are likely to be profoundly positive.

A. A Government That Looks Like America

The most immediate and visible effect of sortition would be a government that actually represents the American people. For the first time in American history, the halls of power would be filled with people who look like, think like, and live like the people they govern. The farmer from Iowa, the nurse from Atlanta, the autoworker from Detroit, the teacher from Albuquerque—these are the people who would be making the laws, setting the budgets, and shaping the policies that affect every American's life.

This descriptive representation would have profound consequences for the legitimacy and trust in government. When people see themselves reflected in their government—when they know that the person making decisions about healthcare has actually struggled to afford a doctor's visit, when the person setting education policy has actually taught in a public school—they are far more likely to trust the process and accept the outcomes, even when they disagree with specific decisions.

B. A Government Free from Corruption

By eliminating the need for campaign contributions, removing the incentive for post-government lobbying, and ensuring that no one can buy their way into power, sortition would drastically reduce political corruption. The revolving door would stop spinning. The influence of corporate money would be broken. The system of legalized bribery that currently defines American campaign finance would be replaced by a system in which no one has anything to gain personally from public service.

This does not mean that corruption would be impossible—no system is immune to human frailty—but it means that the structural incentives for corruption would be eliminated. A randomly selected citizen has no donors to repay, no lobbyist to reward, no political future to protect. Their incentive is to do the right thing, and the evidence from citizens' assemblies suggests that, given the opportunity, most people will.

C. A Government Capable of Long-Term Thinking

One of the most damaging features of the current electoral system is its short-termism. Elected officials operate on two-year or four-year election cycles, which creates a powerful incentive to prioritize immediate, visible results over long-term, sustainable policies. Climate change, infrastructure decay, pension solvency, and other slow-moving crises are perpetually deferred because addressing them requires short-term sacrifice for long-term gain—a trade-off that electoral incentives make nearly impossible.

A sortition-based legislature, freed from the pressure of re-election, would be far better positioned to make long-term decisions in the public interest. Members would not need to worry about how a difficult decision would play in the next election cycle. They could focus on what is right, not what is popular. The evidence from citizens' assemblies supports this: the French Convention on Climate, for example, produced recommendations that were far more ambitious than anything elected officials had been willing to propose, precisely because the assembly members were not constrained by electoral calculations.

D. A More Engaged and Empowered Citizenry

Paradoxically, a system in which political participation is randomly assigned rather than voluntarily chosen is likely to produce a more engaged and empowered citizenry than the current system. When every citizen knows that they could be called upon to serve—that they could be the one making the decisions—they have a powerful incentive to become informed, to pay attention to public affairs, and to think critically about the issues facing their community and their country.

Moreover, the experience of service in a citizens' assembly is transformative. Participants in citizens' assemblies consistently report that the experience deepens their understanding of complex issues, increases their sense of civic efficacy, and strengthens their commitment to democratic participation. If millions of Americans were to serve in sortition-based legislatures over the course of their lives, the cumulative effect on civic knowledge, civic engagement, and civic trust would be enormous.

VII. Conclusion

The American electoral system is broken. It is broken not because the American people are broken, but because the system itself is designed—whether by intention or by the accumulated weight of decades of legal, financial, and institutional choices—to serve the interests of the powerful at the expense of the many. Elections have become a mechanism for laundering oligarchic power through the language of democracy, giving the appearance of popular sovereignty while delivering the reality of elite control.

Sortition offers a way out. It is not a panacea—no system of governance is—but it is a system that is more democratic, more representative, more resistant to corruption, and more capable of producing thoughtful, long-term policy than the electoral system it would replace. It is a system with deep historical roots, strong empirical support, and the potential to restore the promise of democracy to a nation that has strayed far from it.

The choice before us is not between sortition and some idealized version of electoral democracy that has never existed. The choice is between sortition and the actual electoral system we have—a system that is corrupt, polarized, unequal, and increasingly illegitimate in the eyes of the citizens it claims to serve. That is not a difficult choice.

It is time to trust the people. Not the wealthy, not the well-connected, not the professionally political—the people. All of them. Selected at random, given the resources and support they need, and empowered to govern. That is what democracy was always supposed to be. Sortition is how we get there.

The lottery is not a departure from democracy. It is democracy's purest form.

The Case for Sortition

Sortition—selecting legislators or other officials by lottery from the general population—has gained increasing attention as a proposed reform, with advocates drawing on both historical precedent and contemporary political science. Here's a substantive look at the arguments.

Addressing Elite Influence

The core problems with elections:

  • Modern campaigns require enormous fundraising, creating dependency on wealthy donors and organized interests
  • Candidates who succeed tend to come from narrow socioeconomic backgrounds—lawyers, businesspeople, career politicians
  • The "iron law of oligarchy" suggests organized groups inevitably concentrate power regardless of formal democratic structures
  • Revolving doors between government and lobbying create entrenched networks of influence
  • Media dynamics favor photogenic, well-connected candidates regardless of competence

How sortition responds:

  • Random selection makes targeted lobbying essentially impossible—you cannot meaningfully corrupt people you cannot identify in advance
  • It removes the campaign finance pipeline entirely, since there are no campaigns
  • Officials cannot be promised future employment because their tenure is deliberately temporary
  • Selection by lot is structurally impossible to buy access to at the point of decision

Improving Representation

Current democratic deficits:

  • Legislative bodies worldwide skew heavily toward higher income, education, age, and specific professions
  • Self-selection in politics means those who run systemically differ from those they represent
  • Racial, gender, and class diversity in legislatures often fails to match populations
  • Millions feel politically unrepresented because no candidate reflects their circumstances

Sortition's representational advantages:

  • A sufficiently large randomly selected body will, by statistical necessity, mirror the population across virtually every demographic dimension
  • This includes not just visible characteristics but lived experience, worldview, economic pressures, and practical knowledge of ordinary life
  • Stratified sampling can guarantee proportional representation of specific groups
  • It eliminates the "filter" of ambition, charisma, and institutional connections
  • People who would never consider running for office—because they're busy working, parenting, or simply uninterested in politics—become representative voices

Improving Deliberation and Decision Quality

Arguments for cognitive diversity:

  • Scott Page's work on "diverse cognitive toolkits" suggests groups of randomly selected individuals with varied problemsolving approaches often outperform groups of credentialed experts on complex problems
  • Homogeneous groups of experts share blind spots; randomly selected populations bring genuinely different frameworks
  • Ordinary citizens confronting evidence in structured deliberative settings demonstrate substantial capacity for nuanced judgment
  • Citizens' assemblies in Ireland (on abortion, climate, and other issues), France (the Convention Citoyenne pour le Climat), and British Columbia have produced thoughtful, serious recommendations

Reducing perverse incentives:

  • Elected officials face pressure toward short-term thinking driven by election cycles
  • Officials selected for fixed terms with no possibility of reelection are freed from pandering toward the next campaign
  • This arguably allows longer-term decision-making on issues like climate change, pension reform, and infrastructure
  • Deliberation replaces performance as the mode of governance

Deepening Democratic Legitimacy

Addressing democratic disillusionment:

  • Widespread belief that "all politicians are the same" or that "my vote doesn't matter" erodes institutional legitimacy
  • When people see governing bodies that genuinely look like their communities, trust may increase
  • Sortition embodies political equality in its most literal form—every citizen has an equal chance of governing
  • Ancient Athenian democracy, whatever its limitations, used sortition precisely because it was understood as the more democratic method compared to elections (which Greeks associated with aristocracy)

Expanding civic participation:

  • Serving in a governing body becomes a civic duty comparable to jury service
  • It could create a population with direct experience of governance, reducing the perceived distance between citizens and state
  • Millions of people might experience meaningful political participation rather than the thin version voting provides every few years

Serious Objections and Complications

Intellectual honesty requires engaging with significant criticisms:

Competence and Complexity

  • Modern governance involves extraordinarily complex issues—monetary policy, biosecurity, international treaty law, advanced technology regulation
  • Randomly selected individuals may lack the background to evaluate technical information meaningfully
  • Counter from advocates: sortition bodies would have access to expert advisors, briefing materials, and extended deliberation time (unlike legislatures often voting on omnibus bills they haven't read). The question is whether structured deliberation by informed lay people is worse than rushed votes by politicians who are themselves often non-specialists influenced by staff and lobbyists.

Accountability

  • Elected officials can be removed; sortition officials face no electoral consequences for poor decisions
  • Advocate response: fixed terms, transparency requirements, and accountability to subsequent sortition bodies or to judicial review can provide accountability without electoral incentive structures. Also, current electoral accountability is weaker than idealists assume.

Manipulation of the Process

  • Someone controls the lottery, the agenda, the information provided, the rules of deliberation
  • Any power structure can be captured at the level of design rather than at the level of who is selected
  • Stratified sampling requires someone to define the categories
  • This risk is serious and may be sortition's deepest vulnerability: the architecture of the randomly selected body becomes the new terrain of political struggle

Scale and Practicality

  • Sortition worked in Athens with a relatively small citizen body making relatively limited decisions
  • Governing large modern states raises questions about whether a few hundred randomly selected individuals can handle the volume and complexity of legislation
  • Advocates propose hybrid systems—sortition for specific functions alongside elected bodies, or sortition bodies that set agendas while technical drafting is handled by experts

Vulnerability to Demagoguery Within Deliberation

  • Random selection does not guarantee random selection of character traits
  • Some fraction of any population is charismatic and manipulative
  • Internal dynamics of deliberation could be dominated by the most aggressive participants
  • Careful procedural design (trained facilitators, structured deliberation) would be essential

Reasonable Assessment

Sortition is most compelling not as wholesale replacement for all electoral democracy but as a complementary institution—what political theorists call "mixed constitution." The strongest proposals tend to involve:

  • A sortition-based chamber reviewing and approving/rejecting legislation from elected bodies
  • Sortition citizens' assemblies with binding authority on specific complex or long-term issues
  • Sortition oversight bodies for constitutional matters, redistricting, or campaign finance

The most honest assessment is that elections suffer from well-documented, serious failures—particularly regarding representation, elite capture, and accountability—and that sortition addresses several of these structural problems in ways that are difficult to replicate through electoral reform alone. Simultaneously, sortition introduces its own serious risks, particularly around process design and the question of whether removing popular sovereignty over who governs is itself a democratic loss.

The ancient Athenians' deeper insight was arguably not that sortition is perfect, but that no single selection mechanism adequately captures what democracy requires. They used sortition and elections for different purposes, recognizing each institution's strengths and vulnerabilities. That balanced perspective may still be the most productive framework.

“In Defense of Democracy: Why We Must Never Let Random Citizens Ruin Everything”

This is perhaps the most cherished argument: that elections, and only elections, produce competent, experienced leaders.

“Exactly,” the teacher said. “That’s the system working.”

“No,” the sortition supporter said. “Mob rule is when a small, organized minority uses money and media to manipulate a distracted majority. This would be… actual rule by the majority, chosen by lot.”

“Sounds chaotic,” the official said.

“Sounds like power can’t be monopolized by career politicians,” the sortition supporter said. “Which, to you, probably does sound chaotic.”

In the end, the defenders of elections stood firm, united by a profound conviction: that the best way to avoid rule by the unprepared is to ensure rule by the professionally ambitious, lavishly funded, and permanently campaigning.

And so the lottery of citizenship remained, in their eyes, far too dangerous to be trusted with anything more important than jury duty—or choosing which slightly different slogan will be printed on the same old policies.

Because the machinery of elections — the fundraising, the media, the advertising, the lobbying — does not amplify your voice. It dampens it. It turns the volume of popular will down to a whisper while turning the volume of wealth-based influence up to a roar.

We must look at this directly. The election system, as it stands, is not a mechanism for expressing the will of the people. It is a mechanism for containing it.

II. The Ancient Wisdom We Abandoned

"But this is the best system human beings have ever devised!"

I've heard this claim so many times it has taken on the texture of a religious creed. And I want to challenge it — not with theory, but with history.

Because for centuries — for the defining centuries of democratic thought — the world's first democracy did not elect its leaders. It chose them by lot.

Athens. The birthplace of democracy.

In the Athenian system, most government positions — including the powerful Council of Five Hundred, which set the agenda for the entire democracy — were filled not by elections but by random selection from among eligible citizens. They literally used a machine called a kleroterion — a stone slab with slots and colored dice — to select citizens for public service.

And the Athenians were not naive. They did not choose sortition by accident. They did so because they understood something profound about elections — something we have apparently forgotten:

Elections are inherently aristocratic. They select for those who want power. Sortition selects for those who have wisdom.

The great thinkers of antiquity — Aristotle, Pericles, Herodotus — regarded elections as fundamentally oligarchic, as mechanisms that naturally elevate the ambitious, the wealthy, and the well-connected. Sortition, by contrast, was seen as the truly democratic method, because it gave every citizen an equal chance — not an equal theoretical right, but an equal mathematical probability — of governing.

And this was not merely philosophical. The Athenian democracy, powered by sortition, presided over an explosion of culture, philosophy, art, and civic engagement that laid the foundations of Western civilization. It was not perfect — no human system is — but it was radically, genuinely more representative than anything elections have produced in the modern era.

When we abandoned sortition and embraced elections as the sole mechanism of democratic representation, we told ourselves we were choosing merit over randomness. But let me ask you: What merit? The merit of fundraising? The merit of name recognition? The merit of capacity to endure a three-year campaign that feels less like a job interview and more like a gladiatorial contest in which the last politician standing wins the right to be immediately devoured by donors and lobbyists?

I submit that we did not choose merit. We chose familiarity with power. We chose a system that looks democratic but functions as a rotating gerontocracy, a self-selecting political class that governs in its own interest while performing outrage on cable news.

III. How Sortition Works

Now, I can almost hear the objections forming. "Random selection? You want to leave the fate of three hundred thirty million people to a coin flip?"

No. Let me be precise about what sortition actually entails — because the caricature is not the proposal.

First: random selection from a verified citizen pool. Just as we use random selection for jury duty — a Bedrock principle of American justice — we would use it to select legislative assemblies and executive councils. Every eligible citizen has an equal chance of being selected. Not equal in some abstract, rhetorical sense, but mathematically, measurably, provably equal.

Second: stratified sampling to ensure demographic representation. We wouldn't simply pull names from a hat. Modern statistical methods allow us to ensure that the randomly selected body mirrors the population — in age, in race, in gender, in geography, in socioeconomic background, in education, in every dimension that matters for genuine representation. This is not a risk. It is a mathematical guarantee — something that elections, with all their gerrymandering, voter suppression, and structural bias, have never provided.

Third: required service with compensation. Selected citizens would serve for defined terms, paid generously, provided with staff, expertise, and all the information they need to govern thoughtfully — as we do for jurors. Service would rotate. No one would serve indefinitely. The body would be perpetually refreshed — perpetually new blood, new perspectives, new voices.

Fourth: supporting institutions, not legislative chaos. Sortition would not mean a chamber of amateurs stumbling in the dark. Selected citizens would advise alongside professional civil servants, policy experts, and analysts — just as juries consult judges and attorneys. The wisdom would be the citizen's own — rooted in real life, real work, real struggle — informed by expertise rather than replaced by it.

And here is the crucial difference: unlike an elected body, a sortition-based legislature would not owe its position to anyone. It would not have a binder full of favors to repay. It would not owe its next term to a Koch or a Soros or a teachers union. It would owe its position — its only position — to the chance of the draw, and its allegiance would be owed to nothing and no one beyond its own judgment and the common good.

Read that again. Because that is the sentence that separates sortition from every system that has come before.

A government that owes nothing to anyone except the people who chance selected.

That is not chaos. That is freedom.

IV. The Anti-Corruption Revolution

Let us talk about the word — the word that everyone in Washington mouths but no one seems able to cure.

Corruption.

We layer reform upon reform — disclosure requirements, ethics committees, independent prosecutors, campaign finance regulations — and the corruption only deepens. Why? Because we are treating the symptoms while feeding the disease.

The disease is this: elections require money, and money buys power, and power creates more money, and the cycle feeds itself.

You cannot regulate this cycle into submission. You cannot fine it. You cannot hold a hearing on it. You must break the cycle at its root.

Sortition does exactly this. What is the going rate for buying influence over a legislature that no one knows the composition of yet? What does a lobbyist do when there are no campaigns to fund, no candidates to cultivate, no fundraisers to attend?

The answer is simple: nothing. The entire apparatus of political corruption — the donor networks, the revolving door, the PACs, the dark money, the Super PACs, the think tanks that manufacture policy justifications for their benefactors — every single link in that chain is dependent on the existence of elections as the pathway to power. No elections for legislative seats? The chain shatters. Not reforms. Not improves. Shatters.

Think of the implications. The lobbying industry — a 3.7-billion-dollar-per-year enterprise in Washington — exists to influence elected officials who need its money. Replace those officials with randomly selected citizens who have no need for any money — not for campaigns, not for reelection, not for party loyalty, not for media strategy — and what is left? Experts can present evidence to the assembly. They can testify. They can provide data. But they cannot buy the assembly. There is nothing to buy.

This is not utopian. This is just structural. It is the difference between trying to keep a swimming pool clean by filtering the water and simply draining the pool.

V. The Empowerment of Ordinary Citizens

Let's talk about what sortition means — not in theory, but in lived human terms.

Right now, the average American has exactly two channels of political influence: they can vote — once every two years, every four years — for candidates someone else chose. And they can protest — which our government tolerates, more or less, and which it habitually ignores.

Is that power? Really? Is that what the Constitution meant by "We the People"?

Or is it a simulation of power — the feeling of agency without its substance — the political equivalent of a slot machine that pays out just often enough to keep you pulling the lever?

Sortition doesn't simulate power. It distributed power — directly, mathematically, irrevocably. When one in every few hundred citizens serves in a randomly selected legislative body, suddenly democracy is not something you watch on television. It is something your neighbor does. It is something you might be called to do.

Can you imagine the shift? Can you imagine a world in which your coworker, your gym teacher, your postal carrier — ordinary people with calloused hands and complicated lives — have an equal chance to sit in the halls of power, not because they raised money, not because they won a popularity contest, not because they made friends with the right party boss, but because fate chose them?

Can you imagine how that changes the psychology of citizenship? How it transforms the relationship between the governed and the government? How it replaces apathy with expectation, because you know — you know — that someday your name might be called?

The ancient Athenians who served on the Council of Five Hundred did not think of themselves as subjects. They thought of themselves as citizens — not as a legal category, but as an identity, a responsibility, a privilege that belonged to them by birthright. That feeling is what we have lost. And sortition can give it back.

suddenly your neighbor is the representative. Suddenly democracy is not on TV. It's at the kitchen table.

That is empowerment. Not workshops. Not voter drives. Not hashtags. The real, raw, life-altering power of being asked to govern.

VI. The Elephant in the Room — Competence

"But are random citizens qualified to govern?"

I love this question. I love it because it is asked with perfect sincerity by people who look around at the elected Congress and see... competence? Vision? Expertise?

The United States Congress has a public approval rating that has hovered between ten and twenty percent for years. We are governed — to the extent we are governed at all, as opposed to brought to a standstill — by professional politicians whose most demonstrable skills are fundraising, avoiding accountability, and winning elections. These are not skills that translate into governance. Winning an election requires a very narrow set of talents: charisma under lights, the ability to say nothing for hours with confidence, the stomach for a campaign that would send most decent people fleeing, and — above all — the willingness to spend more time with the wealthy than with the governed.

Is that competence?

I would suggest, with great respect, that the most competent governance in America might not be found in the people who have spent decades learning the game of politics. It might be found in the people who have actually lived the consequences of politics. The nurse who has watched the healthcare system fail patients. The farmer who has seen trade policy dictate his livelihood. The small business owner who has been buried in regulatory complexity written by people who have never run a payroll. The teacher who has watched education policy swing like a pendulum driven by partisan winds rather than classroom reality.

Those people understand something that professional politicians — insulated by wealth, staff, and distance — cannot understand. They understand what it feels like to live in the system. And when you give those people access to professional staff, expert testimony, adequate research, and the power to govern — they bring the expertise that no PhD can replicate: the expertise of daily life.

Juries do not require jurors to be legal scholars. They require jurors to be fair-minded citizens — and every single day, in courtrooms across this country, ordinary people deliver verdicts of extraordinary consequence. Not because they planned to. Not because they trained for it. Because they were called to it, and they rose.

Sortition asks of legislative bodies exactly what jury duty asks of courts: that ordinary citizens, informed and supported, can be trusted. Because if we cannot trust the people to govern, then we must honestly say: we do not have a democracy. We have a performance of one.

VII. Breaking the Two-Party Stranglehold

And while we are being honest, let's talk about what has become the most suffocating feature of American political life: the two-party system.

Look at what two parties have given us. Not a marketplace of ideas. A binary. A choice between Red and Blue, served up by media that profits from the conflict and funded by interest groups that profit from the stagnation. Independent candidates are suppressed. Third parties are mocked. The duopoly protects itself with every tool at its disposal — ballot access rules, debate thresholds, gerrymandered districts — while telling you, with a straight face, that you have a choice.

It is monopoly governance dressed in democratic drag.

Sortition breaks the party system by design. There are no parties in sortition. There are no platforms to pledge allegiance to. There are no whips to enforce loyalty. There is only a body of citizens — randomly selected, diverse, free — empowered to deliberate, debate, and decide on the merits of each issue before them.

Imagine, for a moment, a legislature in which members are not bound to "Democrat" or "Republican" but have no party label at all, because they never had to run on one. In which the question is not "What does my party want?" but "What is true, and what is right?" In which the cowardice of partisan loyalty gives way to the courage of independent judgment.

Political polarization is not a natural phenomenon. It is an engineered phenomenon — produced by a system that rewards politicians for stoking division rather than solving problems. Elect a politician whose primary incentive is to raise funds and win the next election, and what you get is a warrior. Select a citizen whose sole purpose is to serve for a defined term and then return home, and what you get is a statesman.

We have been told that the only choices are Republican and Democrat, right and left, conservative and liberal. Sortition reveals the lie. There is a whole spectrum of human thought, experience, and wisdom that the two-party system silences — and sortition brings it back.

VIII. A New Constitutional Foundation

I am not so naive as to suggest that this will be easy. The people who benefit from elections — and make no mistake, there are many who benefit enormously — will fight this with every weapon in their arsenal. They will call it impractical. Unworkable. Un-American.

Un-American?

Let us consult the Americans.

Benjamin Franklin, upon signing the Constitution, described a republic — if we could keep it. Thomas Jefferson warned that "elective despotism was not the government we fought for." John Adams advocated for a government that would be "in miniature, an exact portrait of the people at large." Alexander Hamilton, writing in Federalist No. 68, acknowledged that elections were useful but not without danger — not without the risk of ambition, faction, and corruption.

The founders themselves were uneasy about elections. They embraced them not as an ideal but as a pragmatic necessity in an era without the statistical tools we now possess. Sortition existed in ancient Athens; they knew of it. But the technology of random, representative selection — the science of stratified sampling, the capacity to verify a national population, the ability to support a deliberative body with modern information systems — that technology did not exist.

It exists now.

We don't have to accept the limitations of the eighteenth century. We can honor the founders' values — freedom, equality, republican self-governance — while transcending their methods. We can take the oath "to form a more perfect Union" literally — not as a task completed in one generation, but as an ongoing commitment to get closer, closer, to genuine self-government with each generation's ingenuity.

I am proposing a peaceful, constitutional, democratic transformation — one amendable through the revolutionary innovation of an amendment. Imagine: a citizen body, selected by lot, convened to draft a new amendment — one that establishes citizen juries as the primary legislative assemblies of the nation. Selected like a jury you might serve on next month. Given time, resources, expert staff, full transparency.

Then ratified?

By referendum. Directly. By the people, who would finally have a constitution that says something radical:

We do not entrust our governance to those who seek it. We entrust it to those who are chosen.

IX. A Vision

Close your eyes for a moment. Tomorrow morning, you get a letter. It says:

> "Your name has been drawn by lot from the registered citizens of the United States of America. You have been selected to serve a two-year term in the National Citizens' Assembly. Your salary will be $120,000 per year. You will be provided with housing, expert staff, and all the information you need to deliberate and vote on legislation. Your employer is legally required to hold your position. You are scheduled to begin orientation on September 1st. This is your civic duty, your great honor, and your great privilege."

What would that feel like?

It would feel like being called. It would feel like your citizenship was not a word on a driver's license but a role — enormous, terrifying, sacred.

And across America, in the same week, four hundred and thirty-four of those letters go out. From every walk of life. From every state. From every race, gender, and income bracket. A true cross-section of the Republic — not filtered by party, not auditioned by donors, not tested by the capacity to endure three years of scrutiny that makes the Inquisition look like a spa treatment.

Every person called could say yes or no, for legitimate reasons. But enough say yes — they always have, on juries — and they show up. They sit down next to an electrician from Michigan and a grandmother from Atlanta and a young engineer from Portland and a veteran from rural Mississippi. They are given facts. They are presented with options. They are told: these are the possible laws. Debate them honestly. And decide.

You look around at the body. It looks like America. The faces are the faces of Americans you've seen at the grocery store, at the bus stop, at the school event. For the first time in American history, the faces looking at each other across a chamber of power in Washington would look exactly like the faces of the American people.

And then they craft legislation about healthcare. About war and peace. About immigration. About the climate. About the sprawling, gnarly reality of governing a continental nation.

Those laws would not be shaped by lobbyists. They would not be compromised by party platforms. They would not be sabotaged by members who need to make news rather than make sense.

They could only be shaped by the collective judgment of us. Ordinary, imperfect, extraordinary us — chosen by nothing more than the blind justice of a randomized selection. Governing for a time, and then going home. Again and again. The grab bag. The living delegate lottery. The democracy that this word promised from the start.

X. Answering the Doubters — Honestly

Now, let me be sober. Sortition has challenges. Let me name them plainly and sit with them.

Scale. Ancient Athens was a city-state of perhaps thirty thousand citizens. America is a continental nation of three hundred thirty million. Sortition at this scale requires institutional design that is new. But the principle scales beautifully — citizens' assemblies have operated successfully in Canada, France, Ireland, and elsewhere in recent years, making consequential decisions on everything from climate policy to abortion. We can learn from them and expand.

Manipulation of the pool. If the citizen pool is not truly representative, sortition fails. This requires rigorous, transparent, nonpartisan administration of the selection process — much as we currently do for jury selection, but at greater scale. Independent auditing, statistical verification, public transparency. Hard? Yes. Impossible? No. We census the entire nation every ten years with extraordinary precision. We can randomize a subset with equal precision.

Power vacuum. Some argue that removing elections removes a crucial check on government. But sortition does not remove checks — it redistributes them. Random selection serves as a check on everything elections fail to check: corruption, partisanship, stagnation. And sortition can coexist with other mechanisms — independent courts, free press, direct referenda on fundamental questions — to ensure accountability without recreating the old corruptions.

Public trust. Perhaps the greatest challenge: will people trust a government chosen by lottery? My answer is: do they trust the government we have now? Approval of Congress is in the teens. Trust in government is at historic lows. The question is not whether sortition can build trust — it's whether elections have built trust. And the answer, plainly, is no. Sortition is not a gamble on trust. It is an investment in it — a system whose very structure says to the citizen: you are expected to govern. We believe you can.

That trust, offered freely, is repaid. Every study of citizens' assembly participants shows the same thing: people who serve become more informed, more engaged, more proud of their citizenship. They leave the process saying: I had a say. I mattered. I was heard. That is the seed of trust. Not a ribbon-cutting or a speech. Service.

XI. The Moral Imagination

At the end of the day, this is not a policy argument. It is a moral argument.

It is an argument about whether we believe — deep in our bones, not just in our pocket constitutions — that ordinary people are fit to govern.

Because if we don't believe that, everything else — the elections, the campaigns, the horse race, the red team and blue team — is just theater. Expensive, demoralizing, corrosive theater. We are saying, with every election cycle, that Americans cannot be trusted with power. That power must be earned through a gauntlet that only millionaires and political dynasties can run. That the system must be designed to keep real decision-making in the hands of those who have already proven they can survive the system — which is to say, those who already have power.

It is an elite-filtered power structure that calls itself democracy and wonders why people have stopped believing.

Sortition says something different. Sortition says trust the people. Randomly. Directly. Wholly. Take a nurse and a carpenter and a grandmother and an immigrant and a twenty-something who is still figuring it all out. Put them in a room. Give them information. Give them time. Give them power.

And trust them.

Because the alternative — the thing we have now — is not trust. It is dependence. Dependence on a political class that has failed us, again and again, not from lack of intelligence but from lack of accountability to anything other than the system that elevated it.

XII. Close

John Adams wrote that "no man is wiser than the whole."

He believed the genius of democracy lies not in selecting the best to govern but in finding a way for the many to govern wisely enough. He saw elections as one imperfect instrument among many. Sortition — random selection — is another. And I believe — I know — it is a better one.

Because elections ask people to choose leaders. Sortition asks people to be leaders. And in that transformation — from choosing to being — lies the possibility of a truly democratic nation.

Not a nation run by the well-connected. Not a nation governed by the wealthy. Not a nation where your citizenship is a spectator sport.

A nation where, when the letter arrives — as one day it could, as one day it should — you look at it, and you know that democracy is not something that happens to you once every few years.

It is yours. It is you.

And it is time.

Thank you.

The Lottery of Liberty: Why Sortition Must Replace Elections in America

For over two centuries, the United States has operated under the assumption that electoral democracy is the only viable mechanism for representative government. We are taught to believe that the ballot box is the ultimate instrument of popular sovereignty. However, a closer examination of the modern American political landscape reveals a system in deep crisis. Elections, once envisioned as a bridge between the people and power, have become gatekeepers for oligarchy, engines of extreme polarization, and barriers to genuine civic engagement. It is time to consider a radical, yet historically grounded alternative: sortition, or selection by lot. By replacing elections with the random selection of citizens for legislative and executive roles, the United States can dismantle systemic corruption, dissolve toxic partisanship, and return true power to ordinary people.

The End of Institutionalized Corruption

The most compelling argument for sortition is its ability to eradicate the structural corruption inherent in electoral politics. In the current system, running for office is prohibitively expensive. Congressional campaigns cost millions; presidential campaigns cost billions. This financial barrier creates an immediate dependency: candidates must solicit funds from wealthy donors, corporations, and special interest groups to have any chance of victory. Consequently, elected officials are not accountable to the general public, but to the subset of the population that funds their careers. This is not merely "influence peddling"; it is a feature of the system, not a bug.

Sortition severs this link entirely. If legislators and executives are chosen by random lottery from the citizenry, there is no campaign to fund, no donor to please, and no reelection to secure. A citizen selected to serve does not owe their position to a PAC or a billionaire benefactor; they owe it to chance. This removes the primary incentive for quid-pro-quo corruption. Lobbyists lose their leverage because there is no incumbent to cultivate for future favors. The revolving door between government and industry collapses because public service becomes a temporary civic duty, like jury duty, rather than a career path to lucrative private sector consulting. By removing money from the equation, sortition restores integrity to governance.

Dissolving the Poison of Partisanship

Beyond corruption, elections fuel the hyper-partisanship that has paralyzed American governance. Electoral politics is a zero-sum game designed to divide the populace into opposing tribes. Candidates are incentivized not to find common ground, but to demonize the opposition, mobilize their base through outrage, and prioritize ideological purity over practical problem-solving. This dynamic transforms legislation into a battlefield where compromise is viewed as betrayal. The result is gridlock, where critical issues like healthcare, climate change, and infrastructure remain unaddressed for decades.

Sortition introduces a fundamentally different logic: deliberation over domination. A body chosen by random selection will naturally reflect the demographic and ideological diversity of the nation. It will contain Democrats, Republicans, independents, and apolitical citizens in proportion to their presence in the population. Without the pressure of party primaries or the need to signal virtue to a specific base, these citizens are free to listen, learn, and negotiate. Historical precedents, such as the ancient Athenian Boule and modern citizens’ assemblies in Ireland and Canada, demonstrate that randomly selected groups are capable of reaching nuanced, consensus-driven decisions. When people are not playing to a partisan audience, they are more likely to engage in good-faith debate and prioritize the common good over party victory. Sortition transforms politics from a spectacle of conflict into a workshop of collaboration.

Empowering the Ordinary Citizen

Perhaps the most profound benefit of sortition is its democratizing effect. Elections are elitist by design. They favor the wealthy, the well-connected, the charismatic, and those with the time and resources to campaign. This excludes the vast majority of Americans—working-class individuals, minorities, women, and young people—from holding real power. The political class becomes a self-perpetuating caste, disconnected from the lived experiences of the people they claim to represent.

Sortition shatters this elite monopoly. It operates on the radical premise that any citizen is capable of governing. Just as we trust random citizens to judge their peers in a court of law, we can trust them to legislate and execute laws. Selection by lot ensures that the government looks like the people it serves. A rural farmer, a single mother, a retired teacher, and a young software engineer would have an equal chance of shaping national policy. This inclusivity fosters a deeper sense of civic ownership and trust. When people see themselves reflected in their leaders, legitimacy is restored. Moreover, serving in a sortition-based government would become a universal civic expectation, akin to jury duty, fostering a more informed and engaged populace. Citizens would have a direct stake in the outcome of governance, knowing that they or their neighbors could be called to serve.

Addressing Skepticism: Competence and Accountability

Critics often argue that random citizens lack the expertise to govern complex modern societies. This objection misunderstands the role of legislators and executives. Their job is not to be technical experts in every field, but to represent the values, priorities, and interests of the community. Experts can still advise; agencies can still implement. The key difference is that decisions would be made by representatives of the people, not by career politicians insulated from public consequence. Furthermore, sortition bodies can be structured with support systems—access to non-partisan research, expert testimony, and deliberative facilitation—to ensure informed decision-making.

Regarding accountability, sortition does not mean impunity. Randomly selected officials would serve fixed, non-renewable terms. Their performance would be subject to rigorous oversight by independent bodies, judicial review, and transparent public reporting. Unlike elected officials who can hide behind party lines or blame the opposition, sortition representatives would be directly accountable for their collective decisions. The threat of public scrutiny and historical judgment remains a powerful check on abuse.

Conclusion

The American experiment in electoral democracy has yielded a system that is corrupt, divisive, and exclusionary. It is time to innovate. Sortition offers a path toward a government that is truly of, by, and for the people. By eliminating the influence of money, dismantling the machinery of partisanship, and empowering ordinary citizens to lead, sortition can restore faith in democratic institutions. It is not a utopian fantasy, but a practical solution rooted in historical precedent and modern evidence. The lottery of liberty is not a gamble; it is the surest way to ensure that power resides where it always should have: in the hands of the people.

  • Deliberative Democracy: Randomly selected citizens are typically provided with time, resources, and access to expert testimony to deliberate on issues. This encourages informed decision-making rather than soundbite-driven politics. Studies of citizen assemblies (e.g., in Ireland, Canada, and France) show that ordinary people, when given proper support, can grasp complex issues and reach nuanced compromises.
  • Reduction of Partisan Polarization: Without party labels, individuals are less likely to vote along ideological lines. They are more likely to listen to opposing views and seek consensus, as they are not competing for votes from a partisan base.
  • Long-Term Thinking: Since selected officials do not need to worry about re-election, they are freer to make unpopular but necessary long-term decisions (e.g., climate change mitigation, infrastructure investment, pension reform) without fear of electoral backlash.
  • Equality of Opportunity: Sortition embodies the democratic ideal of political equality—every citizen has an equal chance to hold power, not just those with charisma, wealth, or connections.

4. Practical Considerations and Hybrid Models

Critics argue that random citizens may lack expertise or be vulnerable to manipulation. Proponents counter this by pointing to successful real-world examples:

  • Citizens’ Assemblies: Used in Ireland to debate abortion and marriage equality, and in France to address climate policy. These bodies produced well-reasoned recommendations that were often more progressive and balanced than those of elected parliaments.
  • Jury Duty Analogy: We trust randomly selected citizens to make life-or-death decisions in courts (juries). Proponents argue we can similarly trust them with legislative decisions, especially when supported by experts and facilitators.

Many advocates propose hybrid models:

  • A bicameral legislature where one house is elected (providing accountability and continuity) and the other is selected by sortition (providing representation and deliberation).
  • Sortition used for specific issues (e.g., constitutional reforms, budget prioritization) or for oversight bodies.
  • Executive roles selected by sortition but advised by professional civil servants and expert panels.

Conclusion

Adopting sortition aims to create a government that is more representative, less corrupt, and more deliberative. By removing the incentives of re-election and campaign fundraising, it seeks to restore power to ordinary citizens, ensuring that governance reflects the true diversity and interests of the population rather than the preferences of elites and interest groups. While challenges remain regarding implementation and public acceptance, sortition offers a compelling alternative to the perceived failures of traditional electoral democracy.
